articles.title: India–New Zealand FTA: Government Notifies First Tranche of Customs Duty Concessions; Preferential Tariffs, TRQs and Import Conditions Effective October 20, 2026 - A2Z Taxcorp LLP
articles.summary: India–New Zealand FTA: Government Notifies First Tranche of Customs Duty Concessions; Preferential Tariffs, TRQs and Import Conditions Effective October 20, 2026  A2Z Taxcorp LLP
articles.full_text:
The Ministry of Finance (Department of Revenue), Government of India, has issued Notification No. 32/2026-Customs dated October 16, 2026, notifying the first tranche of tariff concessions under the India–New Zealand Free Trade Agreement (Ind-NZ FTA). The notification, issued under Section 25(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, shall come into force on October 20, 2026.
The notification establishes preferential customs duty treatment for specified goods imported into India from New Zealand, covering concessions in Basic Customs Duty (BCD), Agriculture Infrastructure and Development Cess (AIDC) and Health Cess, as applicable. These concessions are subject to the relevant tariff classifications, product descriptions, value thresholds, quantitative restrictions and prescribed conditions.
Comprehensive Product-Wise Tariff Concessions
Under Table I of the notification, the Government has prescribed preferential customs duty rates for a wide range of tariff lines covering specified agricultural, marine, industrial and other goods. The applicable BCD, AIDC and Health Cess rates have been specified separately for individual tariff classifications.
For instance, imports of fresh, chilled or frozen sheep meat falling under heading 0204 have been assigned a preferential BCD of Nil, AIDC of Nil and Health Cess of Nil. Several specified fish and marine product classifications are also covered by preferential rates, including certain tariff lines carrying a BCD of 25.71%, with Nil AIDC and Health Cess.
The applicable concessions vary across products and tariff lines. Accordingly, importers must examine the precise tariff classification and corresponding rate prescribed under the notification before claiming preferential treatment.
Preferential Customs Duty on Wines Based on CIF Value
Under Table II, the Government has introduced value-based preferential tariff treatment for specified wine products imported from New Zealand.
For the specified tariff classifications covering wines, including sparkling wines and other listed wine products, the notification prescribes the following concessions based on the CIF value of a 750 ml container:
- CIF value of US$5 or above but below US$15: BCD of 20% and AIDC of 75%.
- CIF value of US$15 or above: BCD of 20% and AIDC of 50%.
The preferential rates are subject to the relevant tariff classifications and product descriptions. The notification clarifies that the CIF value shall mean the assessable value determined under Section 14 of the Customs Act, 1962.
Special Preferential Duty Treatment for Kiwifruit and Mānuka Honey
Under Table III, specific preferential duty rates have been notified for New Zealand-origin kiwifruit and Mānuka honey satisfying the prescribed import value conditions.
For kiwifruit falling under HS Code 08105000, having a CIF value of US$2.50 per kg or above, the applicable preferential BCD shall be 15%, with Nil AIDC.
Similarly, Mānuka honey falling under HS Code 04090000, having a CIF value of US$30 per kg or above, shall attract a preferential BCD of 51%, with Nil AIDC, subject to the prescribed certification condition.
For Mānuka honey, the importer must produce a certificate issued by the Ministry for Primary Industries, New Zealand, certifying the imported product as Mānuka honey.
Tariff Rate Quotas Introduced for Mānuka Honey and Albumins
Under Table IV, the notification prescribes Tariff Rate Quota (TRQ) concessions for specified imports, enabling eligible quantities of goods to be imported at the notified in-quota customs duty rates, subject to DGFT authorisation and customs compliance requirements.
For Mānuka honey under HS Code 04090000, having a CIF value of US$20 per kg or above but below US$30 per kg, an initial TRQ quantity of 40 metric tonnes has been notified, with an in-quota BCD of 51% and Nil AIDC.
For albumins falling under HS Codes 35021100, 35021900, 35022000 and 35029000, a TRQ quantity of 200 metric tonnes has been prescribed, attracting an in-quota BCD of 10% and Nil AIDC.
These quantities form part of the initial tariff concession framework under the FTA, with the related quota allocation and implementation procedures governed by the Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT).
Mandatory DGFT Authorisation and Electronic Customs Monitoring
The notification stipulates that importers seeking concessional benefits under the applicable TRQ provisions must obtain authorisation from DGFT in accordance with the relevant procedures prescribed under the Handbook of Procedures, 2023.
The TRQ authorisation must contain the name and address of the importer, Importer-Exporter Code (IEC), relevant Customs Notification number, applicable tariff item, authorised quantity and validity period.
Such authorisations shall be issued electronically by DGFT and transmitted to the Indian Customs EDI System (ICES). Imports against TRQ authorisations shall be permitted only after the corresponding quantities have been debited electronically through ICES.
The electronic authorisation and debit mechanism is intended to facilitate administration and monitoring of the notified tariff quotas.
Rules of Origin Compliance Mandatory to Avail FTA Benefits
A significant condition under the notification is that the preferential customs duty concessions shall be available only for qualifying goods originating in New Zealand.
Importers must establish the origin of imported goods to the satisfaction of the jurisdictional Deputy Commissioner or Assistant Commissioner of Customs, in accordance with the Customs (Administration of Rules of Origin under Trade Agreements) Rules, 2020 (CAROTAR, 2020) and other applicable rules notified by the Central Government.
Accordingly, the mere import of goods from New Zealand shall not automatically entitle an importer to preferential customs duty treatment unless the prescribed origin requirements and relevant conditions are satisfied.
Implementation from October 20, 2026
The concessional customs duty rates and prescribed TRQ provisions under Notification No. 32/2026-Customs dated October 16, 2026 shall become applicable from October 20, 2026.
The notification operates alongside DGFT Public Notice No. 33/2026-27 dated October 17, 2026, which amends Paragraph 2.92 and Appendix 2A of the Handbook of Procedures, 2023, to prescribe the procedural framework for TRQ allocations under the India–New Zealand FTA.
Together, the customs notification and DGFT procedural amendments establish the framework for extending preferential import treatment and administering tariff quotas under the Agreement.
Significance for Indian Importers and Trade
The implementation of the first tranche of tariff concessions under the India–New Zealand FTA represents an important development in bilateral trade policy and preferential customs administration.
The concessions may create additional opportunities for eligible New Zealand-origin goods to enter the Indian market at preferential tariff rates, while the prescribed value thresholds, tariff classifications, quantitative restrictions and origin requirements provide safeguards for administering the concessions.
For Indian importers, customs brokers and businesses engaged in international trade, the notification makes it essential to carefully evaluate HS classification, applicable preferential BCD and cess rates, CIF value thresholds, origin documentation, DGFT authorisation and electronic quota compliance, wherever applicable.
The notification marks an important step in operationalising the first tranche of tariff commitments under the India–New Zealand Free Trade Agreement, with preferential customs duty benefits becoming effective from October 20, 2026.
The Notification can be accessed at: https://taxinformation.cbic.gov.in/view-pdf/1010775/ENG/Notifications

articles.title: China’s non-tariff walls a major export hurdle: FM Nirmala Sitharaman - India Shipping News
articles.summary: China’s non-tariff walls a major export hurdle: FM Nirmala Sitharaman  India Shipping News
articles.full_text:
BANGKOK: Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman on Friday said China’s non-tariff barriers were the biggest hurdle for Indian exports, alleging that Beijing had denied market access to Indian products despite significant demand potential, including for generic drugs, bovine meat and agricultural produce, contributing to a widening trade imbalance. She also called for a review of India’s trade agreement with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), saying its benefits were skewed in favour of the bloc.
“A decade has gone by consistently putting up a case for market access for Indian products but non-tariff barriers have been very strong and China uses non-tariff barriers unhesitatingly. Non-tariff barriers are the biggest hurdle in the trade between India and China,” she said during a conversation hosted by the Atlantic Council on the sidelines of the International Monetary Fund-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok.
India’s trade deficit with China more than doubled to $112 billion in FY26 from $52.7 billion in FY16. Sitharaman said New Delhi had repeatedly sought market access for products in which India had a competitive advantage, but progress had been limited despite scope for discussions on sanitary and phytosanitary measures and other regulatory issues.
Responding to Sitharaman’s remarks, China’s foreign ministry said Beijing was ready to work with New Delhi to address “each other’s economic and trade concerns in a balanced way and promote the steady development of bilateral relations”. “China never aims for trade surplus,” Chinese foreign ministry Spokesperson Mao Ning told media in Beijing, as reported by PTI.
Sitharaman’s comments come days after Commerce Minister Shri Piyush Goyal said India was working to develop relations with China “once again”, while cautioning that the outcome remained uncertain.
“I think we had some concerns in the past. We are working to develop relations with China once again, but the last word has not been scripted on this journey,” he said on Wednesday at the Bloomberg New Economy Forum.
Sitharaman said India had refrained from adopting punitive trade measures to address its trade imbalance with China, preferring negotiations despite the difficulties involved, unlike some other countries. “Probably that’s not the way India believes in dealing with trade negotiations. We sit and talk. It is sometimes very tiresome but we do go through that approach rather than putting countervailing duties or some non-tariff barriers to counter their non-tariff barriers,” she said.
On the skew in trade benefits in favour of Asean, Sitharaman said India needed to reassess the impact of its trade agreement with the bloc, signed more than a decade ago, and refashion it to address the imbalance and its effects on domestic manufacturers and importers. “We need to have that agreement continue but in a slightly refashioned manner. It cannot so adversely affect one side which is the Indian side,” she said. India’s trade deficit with Asean countries crossed $50 billion in FY26.
Sitharaman also defended India’s decision to stay out of the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP), saying the government had not seen sufficient benefits in joining the trade framework. “We took a conscious call to stay out of RCEP because we didn’t think it was going to do any help for us,” she said.
Sitharaman said Indian exporters had turned global trade disruptions into opportunities by identifying alternative markets, including countries that had imposed high tariffs on Indian goods. Exports of goods and services grew 23 per cent in September, she said, citing the performance as evidence of exporters’ resilience amid a difficult global environment.
“Even in this situation Indian exporters have found very many different alternative markets — and even to markets which have literally levied huge tariffs on us — we have reached these markets and very efficiently,” she said.
India remained committed to multilateralism but was accelerating bilateral trade agreements rather than waiting for progress in the global trading system, the minister said. “We believe in multilateralism. However, given today’s environment we are very keen that we build our strength in trade through bilateral agreements as well.”
She cited India’s trade engagements with the European Union, New Zealand, Australia and the United Arab Emirates, as well as negotiations with Canada, saying political will on both sides had helped move long-pending talks forward.
On India-US trade negotiations, following recent comments by Goyal, Sitharaman said: “I hope in the interest of global trade and in the interest of trade between the two partners India and US the trade agreement gets concluded at the earliest.”

articles.title: Political instability is driving Bangladesh's economic collapse - India Today
articles.summary: Political instability is driving Bangladesh's economic collapse  India Today
articles.full_text:
Bangladesh's prolonged political uncertainty is taking a growing toll on its economy, as businesses hesitate to invest and ordinary households struggle with rising costs. With poverty increasing, job creation stagnating and purchasing power shrinking, the crisis extends beyond inflation and global oil prices.
The rising cost of living in Bangladesh is no longer merely a matter of market prices. Its effects have eroded people's real incomes. As a result, they must continually cut back on everyday expenses.
Recent research by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) shows that sharp increases in food and energy prices do not merely generate temporary inflation; the effects of such inflationary crises weigh on a country and its state institutions for a long time. These effects will be prolonged in Bangladesh, too. Poverty has already increased. Many people have fallen below the poverty line. At the same time, employment is contracting and production is declining, and the situation is worsening by the day. The gap between the economically privileged and the disadvantaged is set to widen considerably.
A recent Reuters report on poverty said a new IMF economic model calculated the disproportionately greater impact of inflation on poor households. According to the model, between 2021 and 2024, about 23 million more people fell into extreme poverty than previous estimates indicated. The IMF will publish the research as a chapter in its forthcoming World Economic Outlook.
This warning is particularly important for Bangladesh, because the figures being presented to show that inflation is declining conceal a mathematical sleight of hand. The reported decline in inflation uses 2025 as the comparison year, measuring the current rate against that year's abnormally high inflation. Meanwhile, the IMF model discussed in the Reuters report was developed with politically stable countries in mind. And in those countries, rising energy prices have been treated as the principal cause of inflation.
But in countries such as Bangladesh, Afghanistan, and Myanmar, rising energy prices are not the sole underlying cause of inflation. Moreover, inflation had already become acute in Afghanistan, Myanmar, and Bangladesh before the outbreak of the war between America and Iran.
In Bangladesh, inflation reached alarming levels immediately after Yunus illegally seized power. After Yunus left power, oil prices rose as a consequence of the US-Iran war. In reality, the main reason for inflation in countries like these is that state structures have been dismantled. In Afghanistan, Taliban militants dismantled those structures. In Myanmar, they were broken down through armed rebellions by various ethnic groups and the military’s overthrow of the elected government.
In Bangladesh, too, an NGO figure named Yunus dismantled the structures of the state by bringing together militants and various groups to overthrow a stable government through "meticulous design". Several religious-nationalist political parties helped Yunus dismantle those structures and create anarchy in the country. The starkest example of the dismantling of state structures in Bangladesh is the enactment of a law to protect the killers of police officers instead of bringing them to justice. Judges were even forced to resign through mob violence at the Supreme Court.
Meanwhile, as in Myanmar, a so-called elected government has been formed in Bangladesh under the guise of an election in which only one political grouping participated. Since the election did not reflect public opinion, political stability has, naturally, not followed. Consequently, as in Afghanistan and Myanmar, political instability is the principal reason Bangladesh is being drawn ever further into poverty.
Beyond the parameters of the IMF model, Bangladesh stands alongside Afghanistan and Myanmar in Asia as a country experiencing a more severe rise in poverty and inflation. Here, poverty and inflation will not merely decline slowly; the situation may instead descend into an even deeper crisis.
When energy prices rise and global trade, including the energy trade, shifts onto new paths, every country must confront changing circumstances with considerable caution and competence. Governing at such a time demands a much higher level of capability. Above all, it requires national unity, a stable country, and leadership that commands trust.
At present, as in Myanmar, the activities of Bangladesh's principal political party are banned. The leader of Bangladesh's principal party, the Awami League, is currently in India as a state guest. She has announced through the international media that she will return to the country in December. From this, observers at home and abroad understand that the country is about to enter a new political chapter.
Naturally, therefore, domestic and foreign businesspeople want to get through this period without taking risks. This reluctance among businesspeople to act is pushing Bangladesh further into economic stagnation with every passing day.
The damage Yunus, the NGO leader who seized power, inflicted on the country's military and civilian structures and its economic sector presents the greatest obstacle this government faces in trying to overcome the crisis. In most areas, this government continues to follow Yunus's policies. As a result, it has essentially defined itself as Yunus 2.0. It was not properly elected, with actual participation in the election amounting to only 12% to 15% of voters.
For this reason, rising inflation and poverty in Bangladesh cannot be attributed solely to higher energy prices. Far more consequential are political instability, the government's lack of popular representation, the absence of capable state leadership, and the lack of a clear direction for governing the country.
FROM YUNUS TO THE PRESENT GOVERNMENT: INFLATION REMAINS HIGH
The World Bank's April 2026 Bangladesh Development Update raised similar concerns. The institution reported inflation at around 8.5 percent in the 2026 fiscal year, with prices remaining high for both food and non-food items. As low-income workers' wages failed to keep pace with prices, their purchasing power declined.
In its July 2026 forecast, the Asian Development Bank (ADB) projected inflation in Bangladesh at 9% for 2026 and 8.8% for 2027. It raised its 2027 inflation forecast because it feared the second-round effects of energy and electricity costs would persist.
The IMF's revised October forecast paints a more troubling picture, putting GDP growth at 3.2% and inflation above 10%. The modest easing anticipated in July has thus given way to a forecast of renewed inflationary pressure alongside weak economic growth.
Since July, however, global politics, oil prices, and oil supply routes have become increasingly complicated. A new chapter in the US-Iran war began in September. In this chapter, the Houthis have put another oil transport route, the Red Sea, at risk; by attacking a Saudi airport in October, they have placed Saudi airspace in the same predicament.
As a result, the political and security situation has already become more complicated not only in the Middle East but also in Pakistan. If Pakistan commits itself more deeply to the Mecca agreement, it will find itself in still greater difficulty. Following the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, analysts in Pakistan are saying that the country's political, security, and energy crises will all intensify. Entering a framework such as the Mecca agreement bears much of the responsibility for this predicament.
Bangladesh, meanwhile, has already become more deeply entangled in its relationship with Pakistan. It has expressed a desire to join the Mecca Pact. Bangladesh may therefore have to bear some of the consequences that fall on Pakistan. The more actively Pakistan involves itself in Saudi Arabia, the more it will expose itself as a target for the Houthis and Iran. If Bangladesh continues to support Pakistan openly in this manner at such a time, its energy import routes may face disruption.
In both the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea, the countries of the Mecca Pact and their supporters will face obstruction as part of Iran's and the Houthis' war effort. With its present instability and weak economy, Bangladesh will find it extremely difficult to withstand the pressures of such a situation. The country's stability and international position will become even more precarious.
Above all, with the war entering this new chapter, any assurance that global oil prices will fall has become increasingly implausible. The cost of transporting oil, which stood at $30,000, has now reached $1.2 million. At this moment, the world sees no prospect of that cost falling; it sees only further increases.
It is therefore impossible to reduce inflation or prevent poverty from rising merely by controlling oil prices or thinking in terms of oil alone. What Bangladesh needs first and foremost is capable political leadership to govern the country. From the New Deal to the recovery from recession during Obama's presidency, political decisions shaped the way out of economic crisis.
Economic conditions and available resources alone were not the determining factor. Again, although widely condemned in history, Adolf Hitler brought about economic development in his country after World War l through political decisions, as did Japan's leadership after World War ll.
Even in Bangladesh, when the Awami League-led Grand Alliance formed the government in 2009, the country was facing a severe energy crisis. The world was in recession. The government at the time overcame these difficulties by using political decisions to guide the economy and make energy policy an integral part of it. To overcome the recession, the government set energy production targets, took swift decisions, and began work, despite condemnation from many quarters.
It focused on restoring economic momentum by increasing purchasing power in the domestic marke

articles.title: China imposes export curbs on tunnel boring machines, raising concerns for India’s infrastructure projects - Business Upturn
articles.summary: China imposes export curbs on tunnel boring machines, raising concerns for India’s infrastructure projects  Business Upturn
articles.full_text:
China’s Ministry of Commerce and the General Administration of Customs have announced export controls on tunnel boring machines and related components, alongside restrictions covering specialised excavators and high-altitude concrete-spraying equipment. The measures, announced on Monday, will take effect on November 18 and could complicate procurement for infrastructure projects that rely on Chinese-made machinery. Beijing says the controls are intended to protect national security and national interests.
The move is relevant to India, where tunnel boring machines are used to construct underground metro corridors, railway tunnels and road links through difficult terrain. However, China’s announcement does not specifically name India or establish that any particular Indian project will be delayed. The impact will depend on the equipment involved, applicable licensing requirements and whether alternative suppliers can meet project needs.
The new controls cover full-section tunnel boring machines, including earth-pressure-balance and rock-tunnelling machines, as well as purpose-built components such as cutterheads, screw conveyors, segment erectors and main drive systems. Certain walking excavators and plateau-type wet shotcrete machines are also included. The latter equipment is designed for high-altitude construction, where concrete mixtures must be pumped and sprayed onto working surfaces.
China’s notice sets out different compliance requirements depending on the destination and item. Exports of specified controlled equipment to sensitive countries and regions with which China has disputes require licences. For other destinations, the announcement provides for registration and declarations, alongside undertakings against unauthorised onward transfers to sensitive destinations. Exporters must identify controlled goods accurately in customs declarations, while shipments may be held if authorities question the information supplied.
The announcement also adjusts controls on selected dredging equipment, including slurry pumps, dragheads and cutterheads that meet specified technical thresholds. These items are used to remove underwater sediment during harbour, river and marine construction.
The development comes amid previous concerns over access to tunnelling equipment manufactured in China. In 2024, Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal raised the issue of a German manufacturer facing difficulties exporting tunnel boring machines from China to India, according to contemporary media reports. The latest announcement formalises controls for specified equipment but does not, by itself, confirm a blanket ban on supplies to India.
China’s commerce ministry said qualifying export licence applications would be reviewed under its laws and approved when requirements are met. The next key date is November 18, when the measures take effect. Indian infrastructure developers and equipment suppliers will need to assess sourcing arrangements and possible delivery risks as implementation details emerge.

articles.title: China tightens export curbs on TBM raising fresh concerns over India’s infrastructure projects - PSU Watch
articles.summary: China tightens export curbs on TBM raising fresh concerns over India’s infrastructure projects  PSU Watch
articles.full_text:
New Delhi: China has announced sweeping new export controls on tunnel boring machines (TBMs) and other specialised heavy equipment, raising fresh concerns over India’s dependence on Chinese machinery for critical infrastructure projects, including metro networks, high-speed rail corridors and strategically important tunnels near border areas.
The restrictions, announced by China’s Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) on Monday, will come into effect on November 18. Beijing has justified the move on grounds of national security and protection of its strategic interests.
However, the decision raises uncomfortable questions for India, which continues to depend on foreign suppliers for several categories of sophisticated infrastructure equipment despite its ambitious push for domestic manufacturing under the Make in India initiative.
India’s infrastructure ambitions face fresh uncertainty
Tunnel boring machines are critical to the construction of underground metro corridors, railway tunnels and other major infrastructure projects. Any disruption in their availability could affect project schedules, increase procurement costs and complicate the execution of ongoing and proposed projects.
The latest restrictions are particularly significant because China has previously obstructed the supply of TBMs to India.
In 2024, Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal raised the issue with German Vice Chancellor Robert Habeck, pointing out that Beijing was preventing a German company manufacturing tunnel boring machines in China from exporting them to India.
The episode exposed a major vulnerability in India’s infrastructure supply chain: even machinery supplied by European companies can become subject to Chinese restrictions when manufacturing facilities are located in China.
The latest controls could deepen that vulnerability, although their actual impact will depend on licensing decisions, the equipment covered and the availability of alternative suppliers.
Strategic implications for border infrastructure
The restrictions extend beyond conventional tunnelling machinery to include walking excavators and plateau-type wet shotcrete machines, both used in difficult terrain.
Walking excavators are designed to operate on steep, uneven and otherwise inaccessible surfaces, while plateau-type wet shotcrete machines are used for concrete spraying operations in high-altitude environments.
These machines can be important for infrastructure construction in mountainous regions, including areas along India’s sensitive northern borders.
The decision therefore raises strategic concerns at a time when India is expanding road, rail and tunnel connectivity in difficult Himalayan terrain.
While China has not explicitly identified India as a target of the latest measures, the restrictions demonstrate how control over specialised machinery can potentially become an instrument of geopolitical leverage.
Beijing has also tightened export controls on specified dredging equipment, including slurry pumps, dragheads and cutterheads.
The restrictions cover slurry pumps with inlet diameters of at least 0.55 metres and maximum rotational speeds of 400 revolutions per minute, along with certain large pump casings and impellers.
Controls will also apply to dragheads used in trailing suction hopper dredgers and cutterheads deployed in cutter suction dredgers that meet specified technical thresholds.
Such equipment is important for port development, harbour maintenance, maritime infrastructure and underwater excavation.
For India, which is pursuing major port expansion and maritime connectivity programmes, restrictions on specialised dredging components could introduce another layer of supply-chain uncertainty.
The latest announcement follows a draft proposal released by MOFCOM on Friday seeking additional export restrictions on 14 technologies across sectors including artificial intelligence, biotechnology and photovoltaic solar power.
Together, these measures point to China’s increasing use of export controls over advanced technologies and specialised industrial equipment.
Under the new rules, exporters must obtain licences from MOFCOM under China’s Export Control Law and regulations governing dual-use items.
Exporters will also have to declare the relevant control codes and provide detailed technical specifications. Chinese customs authorities can hold shipments pending verification of the information submitted.
This licensing framework gives Beijing greater oversight of sensitive equipment exports and could create uncertainty for overseas buyers even where shipments are not explicitly prohibited.
China’s latest move should serve as a warning for India’s infrastructure planners and policymakers.
India has committed substantial public investment to expanding highways, railways, metro networks, ports and strategic border connectivity. Yet dependence on imported specialised machinery remains a potential weakness in the execution of these projects.
The bigger question is whether India’s domestic manufacturing ecosystem has developed the technological capabilities needed to reduce this dependence.
An export licensing requirement is not the same as an outright export ban. Nevertheless, China’s ability to delay, scrutinise or deny shipments of critical machinery highlights the risks of concentrated supply chains.
For New Delhi, the challenge is no longer limited to securing alternative suppliers. It must also accelerate domestic design, manufacturing and servicing capabilities for advanced tunnelling, excavation and dredging equipment.
Otherwise, India’s ambitious infrastructure expansion could remain vulnerable to decisions taken in Beijing.
The larger concern is straightforward: Can India claim strategic infrastructure independence when access to some of the machines needed to build that infrastructure remains subject to another country’s export approvals?

articles.title: India-US tariff standoff: Why New Delhi must balance trade interests with strategic autonomy | Hindustan Times - Hindustan Times
articles.summary: India-US tariff standoff: Why New Delhi must balance trade interests with strategic autonomy | Hindustan Times  Hindustan Times
articles.full_text:
This article is authored by K P Vijayalakshmi.
India and the US face renewed tariff tensions even as strategic cooperation deepened over the last decade. Recurring trade disputes, particularly at times of severe global crises, is a major irritant for both in the management of bilateral as well as global economies. More importantly, economic friction when colliding with geopolitical alignment has renewed the importance of sustained negotiation.
Since 2004, deepening strategic convergence has supported expanding commercial ties despite a persistent US goods deficit. Revised US Census data show that, in July 2025, US goods exports to India were $3.418 billion, while imports were $9.161 billion. Total bilateral trade in goods and services reached $241.66 billion in 2025. At the same time, shared concerns about China strengthened Indo-Pacific cooperation, illustrating how commercial friction and strategic alignment can coincide.
India’s central challenge is to manage persistent trade irritants without compromising its geopolitical interests. This requires focused negotiations, supply-chain diversification, and deeper cooperation in critical sectors such as pharmaceuticals, technology, energy, and defence.
US–India tariff tensions reflect a longstanding divide between India’s development-oriented economic policies and the American preference for freer trade. From the 1950s through the 1980s, India relied on high tariffs, licensing, and import substitution. Washington viewed these measures as trade barriers, while New Delhi defended them as necessary for industrialisation, economic sovereignty, and protection of infant industries.
After the 1991 economic reforms, India progressively lowered barriers and opened its market to US goods. The 2008 civil nuclear agreement accelerated strategic ties, while expanding commerce added economic weight to the partnership.
Deeper engagement, however, did not eliminate trade friction. Disputes and negotiations continued across agriculture, textiles, pharmaceuticals, medical devices, information technology, intellectual property, and industrial goods. Since 2000, many disagreements have entered the WTO framework, showing that growth in commercial ties has not displaced protectionist pressures in either country.
The conflict is more than an economic quarrel. It illustrates differing issues that have produced prolonged negotiations. Both approach it differently: While Washington combines market-access demands with forceful bargaining, India responds through pragmatism, selective resistance, and cooperative signaling. The sharpest escalation came during the first Trump administration.
In 2018, the US imposed national-security tariffs on steel and aluminium, including imports from India. New Delhi retaliated against selected U.S. products, including almonds, apples, and walnuts. In 2019, Washington removed India from the Generalised System of Preferences, ending duty-free access for several Indian exports and intensifying bilateral bargaining.
India has recently agreed to lower or remove tariffs on a variety of US industrial items, agricultural products (including tree nuts, fruits, and soybean oil), and technological products as part of an ongoing interim trade agreement.
Recurring tariff disputes thus test whether both sides can balance commercial interests with their geopolitical partnership and sustain bipartisan support for Indo-US relations in both countries.
Due to recent changes in US trade policy and legal modifications, the US currently imposes a temporary 10% duty on numerous qualified Indian imports. The decrease to 10% came after India changed its foreign trade regulations pertaining to supply chain norms, substituting the high punitive rates associated with former trade and oil disputes.
Current pressures also reflect links between supply-chain shifts, competition with China, energy security, and India’s Russian oil purchases. The Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 passed the Senate 86–11 on August 7 and the House 262–159 on September 16. It authorises tariffs of up to 100% on major buyers of Russian energy. Although India is not singled out, the measure could constrain its effort to secure affordable supplies.
The US nevertheless remains a major export market and a vital partner in defence, critical technologies, space, education, semiconductors, critical minerals, and Indo-Pacific cooperation. India must therefore protect its export interests while preserving strategic autonomy and preventing trade disputes from weakening the broader relationship.
India has reiterated its obligation to provide 1.4 billion people with energy security. It has promised to safeguard national economic interests in conjunction with industry while informing US interlocutors of the law's potential effects on bilateral relations and international energy markets. While maintaining firmness, this balancing approach should refrain from escalatory rhetoric.
India should refine this approach through five mutually reinforcing measures.
First, pursue targeted negotiations. India should seek product-specific exemptions or lower duties where its exports support US consumers and supply chains. Priorities include textiles, pharmaceuticals, gems and jewellery, leather, marine products, engineering goods, and auto components.
Second, keep retaliation selective. Retaliation may raise input costs, burden consumers, and disrupt US technology, investment, defence, and education links. Tariffs should remain a calibrated negotiating instrument rather than an automatic reaction.
Third, protect vulnerable exporters while improving competitiveness. Labour-intensive and MSME-heavy sectors need time-bound support through faster tax refunds, working-capital assistance, export-credit guarantees, logistics support, and export insurance. Relief should cushion sudden order losses without becoming a permanent subsidy and should accompany reforms in productivity, infrastructure, and standards.
Fourth, diversify markets and deepen political engagement. India should expand trade with the EU, UK, UAE, Australia, Japan, Africa, and Southeast Asia. Simpler rules-of-origin procedures, MSME guidance, export help desks, and quality-certification support would improve use of trade agreements. Additionally, continued engagement with the US Congress, industry, and policy institutions can sustain support for the partnership.
Fifth, expand sectoral cooperation. Pharmaceuticals, semiconductors, critical minerals, clean energy, digital technology, and defence manufacturing offer scope for joint production, trusted supply chains, and regulatory coordination that favour stability over recurring tariff confrontation.
US-India trade friction is longstanding, but commercial trade and investments are embedded in a strategic partnership. India should, therefore, combine negotiation, selective retaliation, exporter support, market diversification, competitive reforms internally while enhancing critical-sector cooperation with strategic partners such as the US. This approach would protect exports while preserving strategic autonomy and the relationship’s value.
(The views expressed are personal)
This article is authored by K P Vijayalakshmi, professor and head of the Department of Geopolitics and International Relations, Manipal Institute of Social Sciences, Humanities and Arts, Manipal Academy of Higher Education.

articles.title: Trump's Russia sanctions waiver eases India's energy woes, lifts trade deal chances - A News
articles.summary: Trump's Russia sanctions waiver eases India's energy woes, lifts trade deal chances  A News
articles.full_text:
US President Donald Trump's waiver of Russian sanctions eases energy concerns for India, one of the top importers of Russian oil, and may improve the chances of New Delhi and Washington agreeing on a trade deal, besides helping overall ties.
An executive order issued by Trump on Friday waived key Russia-related US sanctions and tariffs — including duties on the country's goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas — that had been scheduled to start this week under the legislation known as the Graham Act.
Trump said the waiver was in the national interest of the United States.
The legislation would have exposed Indian goods to stiff tariffs of up to 100% as India is one of the five largest importers of Russian oil and posed a challenge for the Asian nation's energy policies.
Prime Minister Narendra Modi's administration warned last month the new tariff measures on Russia could hurt bilateral ties, adding to diplomatic strain and trade uncertainty.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who arrives in India on Tuesday, said trade talks with New Delhi were a consideration for Trump's decision.
"We are trying to finalise a trade deal with India right now and we are very close to doing that. So, that's one of the things we take into consideration when the President makes a decision about national security waivers," Rubio told reporters in Uzbekistan on Monday.
India is the world's third-largest oil importer and consumer. Earlier this year, Russia accounted for nearly half of the country's oil imports, but purchases fell in August and continue to decline.
Persistently cutting Russian oil imports to avoid new US tariffs risks pushing up fuel prices ahead of regional elections in India, or straining government finances.
"For some countries it is very difficult to acquire energy from alternative sources," Rubio said.
Rubio's two-day visit to India will include a meeting with foreign minister S. Jaishankar on Tuesday to discuss bilateral cooperation, including energy, trade and investment, and defence.
A trade deal between India and the United States has been in the making for months but could not be finalised as talks stalled in part due to complications from the new tariff threat.
"The decision to pause on Russia sanctions could be the confidence-building measure that gives the two sides the negotiating space to get over the final hump," said Michael Kugelman, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council in Washington.
A trade deal has also been held back because Washington is yet to complete a Section 301 trade investigation into several nations, including India, over alleged excess manufacturing capacity. Section 301 is a US trade law that allows retaliation against unfair foreign trade practices.
Earlier this month, India joined a US-led initiative to act against structural overcapacity, along with a few other nations.
Trade officials in New Delhi last week said an agreement with the US was nearly done and expressed optimism over securing a tariff lower than those of competing countries — a longstanding Indian expectation from the deal.
"It (the waiver) provides an important opening and at a critical moment" after renewed tensions over the sanctions bill and new US visa policies had put the relationship "in danger of falling into even harder times," Kugelman said.

articles.title: India-US trade deal influenced Trump to waive Russia oil sanctions, Rubio says - India Weekly
articles.summary: India-US trade deal influenced Trump to waive Russia oil sanctions, Rubio says  India Weekly
articles.full_text:
Highlights:
The United States considered its nearly finalized trade deal with India when deciding to waive sanctions targeting buyers of Russian oil, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday (19), signaling how energy security and bilateral economic ties are shaping Washington’s approach to New Delhi.
“We’re trying to finalise a trade deal with India right now. We’re very close to doing that. So that’s one of the things we’ve taken into consideration..” Rubio said during a press conference in Uzbekistan on Monday (19).
His remarks offer a significant indication that India-US trade negotiations were among the factors considered in Washington’s decision to pause provisions of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. The move has eased the immediate threat of steep US tariffs linked to purchases of Russian oil, a major point of contention between the two countries.
For India, the decision comes amid mounting pressure to secure affordable energy supplies while managing rising domestic inflation. It also offers a potential opening for New Delhi and Washington to resolve a key obstacle to their trade agreement.
Why India’s Russian oil purchases matter
India’s dependence on imported energy has made Russian crude a sensitive issue in its relationship with Washington. The United States has sought to pressure Moscow over its war against Ukraine, while India has maintained that its energy procurement decisions must account for domestic requirements, market conditions and the availability of alternative suppliers.
Rubio acknowledged that countries face different constraints when sourcing energy and said those realities must inform US foreign policy.
“We have had to waive sanctions over the past few months, looking at the global supplies, looking at global prices, and the impact it was having on other countries. I know diesel prices are high in the United States, but they’re really, really high in a bunch of other countries around the world, and then we have to manage all of these things,” he said.
He added that replacing Russian energy supplies is not equally straightforward for every country.
“That’s not an excuse, but all that has to be balanced when you make foreign policy,” Rubio said.
His comments suggest that Washington’s approach is being shaped not only by its objective of pressuring Russia but also by the economic consequences of restricting energy supplies for countries that rely on them.
Trade negotiations and energy security intersect
The potential trade agreement has gained added importance as both governments work to narrow their differences over tariffs and market access. The threat of 100 per cent US tariffs linked to Russian oil purchases had emerged as a major sticking point in negotiations.
Rubio emphasized that Washington’s foreign policy calculations extend beyond the Russia-Ukraine conflict.
“The foreign policy of the United States, of course, takes into account what’s happening with the war between Russia and Ukraine, but it is not solely dominated by that. It hasn’t taken into account a variety of other factors, including our bilateral relationships with other countries, and what they realistically are capable of being able to do in terms of their own energy supplies. You also can’t unravel the economy of other countries because of one central issue. So that’s the complex part of having to balance all this,” he said.
For New Delhi, the comments reinforce the importance of framing energy purchases as a matter of national economic stability rather than solely as a geopolitical choice.
India’s Ministry of External Affairs has said the government remains committed to ensuring energy security “through diversified sourcing and based on evolving market dynamics.” It has also said the implications of the proposed US legislation for bilateral relations and global energy markets were raised in discussions with American representatives.
Rising fuel prices add pressure
The sanctions decision comes as both countries face domestic concerns over energy costs and inflation. In the United States, diesel prices averaged $6.18 per gallon as of October 12, up from $3.48 at the beginning of the year, according to figures cited by the Council on Foreign Relations and the US Energy Information Administration.
India is also facing inflationary pressures. Retail inflation rose to 5.54 per cent in September from 4.83 per cent in August, while food inflation increased to 7.74 per cent, according to the figures cited in the report.
Higher energy costs can place additional pressure on households, businesses and policymakers, making access to reliable supplies an important economic consideration for New Delhi.
Rubio is expected to visit Mumbai on October 20 for talks with India's external affairs minister S. Jaishankar. The discussions will take place as both countries seek to advance their trade negotiations and manage differences over India’s energy ties with Russia.
While Rubio’s remarks do not confirm that a trade agreement is imminent or that the sanctions waiver guarantees a final deal, they make clear that Washington has considered its relationship with India in weighing its Russia-related policy. For New Delhi, the immediate priority remains securing energy supplies while converting the diplomatic opening into progress on trade.

United States Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that Washington was "very close" to finalizing a trade agreement with India, as the Trump administration weighs energy security concerns and Russian oil purchases alongside bilateral trade negotiations.
"We're trying to finalize a trade deal with India right now. We're very close to doing that," Rubio said in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, where he was meeting Central Asian officials ahead of a three-day visit to India beginning Tuesday.
Rubio said the negotiations were among the considerations behind Washington's decision to waive sanctions related to Russian oil and gas, citing concerns about global energy supplies and prices.
"We have to manage all of these things. We're trying to finalize a trade deal with India right now. We're very close to doing that. That's one of the things we take into consideration when the President (Donald Trump) makes a decision about national security waivers and things of that nature," he said.
The secretary of state acknowledged that countries faced different challenges in securing reliable energy supplies.
"Geography is real. For some countries, it's very difficult to acquire energy from alternative sources. That's not an excuse, but all of that has to be balanced when making foreign policy," Rubio said.
Washington and New Delhi announced in February that they had agreed on the terms of an interim trade framework aimed at resolving longstanding bilateral disputes.
Indian Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal said last week that the first phase of the agreement had been finalized and was undergoing legal drafting.
"We hope to be able to finalize that soon and operationalize that once we get the comparable advantage or competitive advantage over our peer countries," Goyal said at an event in New Delhi.
Trade tensions between the two countries escalated last year after President Donald Trump's administration imposed tariffs of up to 50% on Indian goods, partly in response to India's continued purchases of Russian oil during the war in Ukraine.
Washington subsequently lifted the additional 25% tariffs imposed on Russian energy imports.
However, legal challenges in U.S. courts involving Trump's tariff policies have created uncertainty over when the proposed bilateral agreement could take effect.
The United States and India, which maintain a comprehensive global strategic partnership, recorded approximately $149.4 billion in bilateral trade last year.
Following his meetings in Uzbekistan, Rubio will travel to India on Tuesday for a three-day visit, his second trip to the country this year.
He is expected to visit Mumbai, India's financial center, before traveling to Jamnagar in the western state of Gujarat.
Jamnagar is home to the world's largest single-site oil refinery complex.
The visit comes as Washington seeks to deepen economic cooperation with India while balancing its broader sanctions policies and global energy supply concerns.
U.S. Ambassador to India Sergio Gor, who was born in Uzbekistan, also serves as Washington's special envoy for Central Asia.
Rubio arrived in Uzbekistan's historic Silk Road city of Samarkand late Sunday for talks with officials from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.
His delegation includes approximately 200 business executives, reflecting Washington's interest in expanding commercial and energy cooperation across the resource-rich region.
The five former Soviet republics held talks with Trump at the White House in November 2025.
Before beginning formal discussions, Rubio was scheduled to visit Samarkand's historic old city, once an important trading center connecting China and the West.
"This is an important relationship," Rubio said before departing for the region.
"There's countries you'd like to get to because we want to build our relationships with them," he added.
A senior State Department official said Friday that the visit demonstrated Washington's commitment to a "deepening partnership across Central Asia," particularly in the energy sector.
Central Asian countries retain longstanding economic and security ties with Russia, including energy pipelines, migration networks and defense relationships.
However, Moscow's influence has weakened since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, while China has expanded its economic footprint across the region.
China is now the largest trading partner of all five Central Asian countries.
Chinese companies have also pursued major energy and natural resource agreements, including natural gas purchases from Turkmenistan, uranium supplies from Kazakhstan and rare earth mineral projects in Tajikistan.
Rubio's visit comes as Washington seeks to strengthen its presence in a region increasingly important for energy security, critical minerals and strategic competition with Beijing.
The diplomatic tour also follows an increase in Rubio's international travel amid the U.S. war with Iran, continuing fighting in Ukraine and preparations for November's congressional midterm elections.

articles.full_text:
US treasury secretary Scott Bessent has accused European countries of refusing Washington's request to impose secondary tariffs on 
India and China
 for purchasing Russian oil, questioning why the United States should bear the burden of pressuring Moscow alone.
Speaking to NBC News' Meet the Press on Sunday, Bessent said the Trump administration had approached European allies in the spring to seek coordinated action against countries buying Russian energy.
“So we have asked—in the spring, I asked our European allies to join us in putting secondary tariffs on China, on India. They refused. So why should the US bear the burden?” Bessent said.
He added that Washington could re-engage with its European partners, reiterating that President Donald Trump wanted to end the Russia-Ukraine war.
“President Trump has made it clear he wants the killing to stop. And the so-called Graham bill gives the president the flexibility, gives him 60 days to assess the situation,” Bessent said.
US defends 60-day pause on sanctions legislation
Bessent's remarks came after Trump temporarily waived certain provisions under the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, giving his administration 60 days to assess the potential consequences of imposing sanctions and tariffs.
Defending the decision, Bessent insisted that the administration had not lifted sanctions on Russia.
“No sanctions were lifted on Friday,” he told NBC's Meet the Press, referring to Trump's executive order granting the waiver.
The legislation, which received strong bipartisan support in Congress, provides for tariffs of up to 100 per cent on goods imported into the United States from countries that are among the largest buyers of Russian-origin crude oil or natural gas, including India and China.
Bessent said the pause would allow the administration to evaluate the situation before deciding on further measures. He also defended Trump's record on Russia, citing sanctions imposed on Russian energy companies Rosneft and Lukoil.
“President Trump sanctioned the two largest Russian energy companies, Rosneft and Lukoil, which dealt a catastrophic blow to the Russian energy industry,” he said. “So no one has been tougher on Russian sanctions than President Trump.”
US secretary of state 
Marco Rubio
 also defended the pause, saying the administration needed time to assess the consequences of imposing sanctions and tariffs on the global and American economies.
“I think the president wants to take the 60-day period of time to sort of analyse what imposing both sanctions and tariffs will mean to the global economy, and even to the US economy,” Rubio told reporters on Saturday.
Rubio said the administration was also considering pressures on global energy supplies arising from the Iran war, attacks by Houthi militants in Saudi Arabia and the ongoing conflict between Russia and Ukraine.
Bessent accuses Europe of financing Russia's war effort
Bessent also criticised European countries for continuing to purchase Russian oil and gas while supporting Ukraine.
Citing shipments from Russia's Yamal facility, he said 140 cargoes had left during the first six months of the year, with 136 going to European countries, including Belgium, Spain, France and the Netherlands.
Those shipments were worth more than $8 billion, he said.
“The Europeans have given Russia and Vladimir Putin more money than they've given the Ukrainians. They continue to gorge on Russian energy,” Bessent said.
He added that the United States imported $4 billion worth of Russian products, including $1.8 billion in fertilisers, while European countries imported more than 10 times as much.
Bessent also pointed to the UK's decision in May to waive its embargo on diesel and jet fuel made using Russian crude, questioning why similar criticism had not been directed at other countries.
Rubio calls India an important ally
Rubio said Washington needed to consider the energy requirements of countries such as India before deciding whether to impose tariffs or sanctions.
“These sanctions were not just sanctions on Russia. They include tariffs on a number of countries—India, for example, and others,” Rubio said.
He added that countries such as India had diversified their energy supplies but could not immediately stop importing Russian energy.
The comments came amid criticism of Trump's decision to pause enforcement of the sanctions legislation. Indian-American lawmakers Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam criticised the move, arguing that it weakened pressure on Russia and undermined Congress' authority.
Bessent questioned over whether Ukraine is a US ally
During the same NBC programme, Bessent was asked three times whether the United States considered Ukraine an ally. He did not give a direct yes-or-no answer.
“We provide the three different things ... to Ukraine, so that’s what you do for an ally. We’re not providing those to Russia,” he said on the second occasion.
Bessent said Washington supported Ukraine by providing intelligence, Starlink support and allowing Nato countries to purchase American weapons for transfer to Kyiv.
He also questioned why European members of Nato had not supplied Ukraine with more Patriot missile systems, arguing that they had the capability to do so.
His comments followed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's appearance on the programme, during which he warned that it would be a “historic mistake” for the United States to side with Russia.
“We want to trust him, and I hope that he will change his decisions because I think that it's all mistakes, and it will not help us, and it will not help the United States,” Zelensky said of Trump.
Bessent criticised the Ukrainian president for publicly accusing Washington and Elon Musk of restricting resources used by Ukrainian forces. He called the allegations “very reckless”, according to NBC News.
Bessent maintained that Trump wanted to end the war through a negotiated settlement, saying the conflict had to stop and that the president was working towards that outcome.

articles.title: Trump's Russian oil tariff waiver offers India relief, but experts warn of renewed US pressure - Times of Oman
articles.summary: Trump's Russian oil tariff waiver offers India relief, but experts warn of renewed US pressure  Times of Oman
articles.full_text:
New Delhi: US President Donald Trump's decision to waive additional tariffs of 100 per cent on major buyers of Russian oil has provided immediate relief to India, reducing the risk of fresh trade penalties and offering Indian refiners greater flexibility in crude purchases. However, experts warned that the benefits remain uncertain and will depend on global oil prices, supply conditions and future US trade policy.
Trump signed an Executive Order on Friday implementing the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, while simultaneously waiving several sanctions and additional duties under the legislation.
The order provides for additional tariffs of 100 per cent on goods from the five largest importers of Russian crude oil and natural gas making fresh purchases from October 18, but suspends their application through a presidential waiver.
"Pursuant to section 115(a) of the Graham Act, I hereby waive the application of any duties provided for in sections 112 and 113 of the Graham Act or this order," the White House Executive Order stated.
The waiver has no fixed expiry date and can be withdrawn, while existing Russia-related sanctions under other Executive Orders remain unaffected.
According to the Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI), the decision provides India temporary relief but leaves open the possibility of Washington restoring tariff pressure during future trade negotiations.
In its report titled "U.S. Waives Russian-Oil Tariffs: Temporary Relief for India, but Uncertainty Remains," GTRI said, "For India, the waiver buys time but offers no lasting certainty."
R Ramachandran, former Director (Refineries) at Bharat Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL), told ANI that the immediate benefit for Indian oil companies would be greater crude sourcing flexibility rather than necessarily higher refining margins.
"So more than the GRM, what actually impact it will have on Indian refineries will be the availability of more crude choices," he said.
Gross refining margin (GRM) refers to the difference between the value of petroleum products produced by a refinery and the cost of crude oil processed.
Ramachandran explained that increased Russian crude availability could help refiners secure more economical supplies, depending on discounts. However, lower crude prices could also be accompanied by falling petroleum product prices, limiting gains in refining margins.
Rajani Sinha, Chief Economist at CareEdge, said Russia's importance to India has increasingly shifted from discounted oil towards ensuring uninterrupted supplies.
"The discount has really reduced significantly. But yes, what is more important for India now is availability and ensuring consistent supply of crude oil for the economy," Sinha told ANI.
She said Russia's share of India's crude imports had exceeded 30 per cent in recent years, although its price advantage over international benchmarks had narrowed.
GTRI noted that Russia's share in India's oil imports declined from 51 per cent in July to 44 per cent in August as purchases shifted towards the United States and the United Arab Emirates.
The think tank also highlighted Washington's own energy requirements as a possible factor behind the waiver.
According to its report, the United States agreed to purchase Russian diesel under an October 9 agreement to address domestic fuel shortages and elevated prices.
It also noted that Washington had agreed not to raise tariffs on China until January 10, suggesting that targeting India alone could complicate ongoing bilateral trade negotiations.
"The message is clear: U.S. interests determine when penalties apply, while the ability to retaliate helps secure protection," GTRI founder Ajay Srivastava said in the report.
Meanwhile, Ramachandran said a sustained waiver could help reduce freight costs and ease logistical constraints associated with Russian oil shipments.
He said greater vessel availability and smoother payment arrangements could improve crude procurement economics.
"If Russia and India can agree upon on a continued ruble-rupee exchange for this, it also supports to ease the foreign exchange outgo which currently is affecting the Indian Rupee's strength," he said.
However, these benefits would depend on the restrictions that remain applicable.
On the broader economic impact, Sinha said India's current account deficit could remain manageable despite elevated crude prices, supported by merchandise and services exports.
She expects the current account deficit to remain between 0.8 and 1.2 per cent of GDP, assuming crude prices range between USD 80 and USD 100 per barrel during the remaining financial year.
However, persistently higher prices could widen the deficit towards 1.5 per cent of GDP under adverse conditions.
Sinha expects average inflation of around 5 to 5.5 per cent, although higher fuel costs and food inflation remain risks.
She said the fiscal impact would depend on whether elevated oil costs are absorbed through excise duty reductions, oil marketing companies or higher retail fuel prices.
Healthy tax collections and potential disinvestment receipts, including from IDBI Bank, could help the government manage fiscal pressures, she added.
On the rupee, Sinha said the waiver could improve market sentiment but was unlikely to provide substantial direct support to the currency.
She also stressed that a lasting India-US trade agreement would offer greater economic stability than temporary tariff relief, warning that fresh US tariff threats could emerge.
Ramachandran cautioned against immediately entering long-term Russian crude supply agreements without clarity on the waiver's duration.
"The first thing I would say is that it is too early to look at jumping into long-term contracts," he said.
He added that refiners would need to assess whether Russian crude discounts and stable supply conditions could be sustained.
GTRI similarly warned India against making permanent trade concessions in exchange for temporary relief.
"India should protect its energy security, buy oil on commercial terms and prepare for renewed U.S. pressure. Temporary tariff relief is no basis for permanent trade concessions," Srivastava said.

articles.title: ACIC-VGU Invites Startup Applications for MeitY's GENESIS Pilot 2.0: Funding Support of Up to 40 Lakh Available - India's News.Net

VMPL
Jaipur (Rajasthan) [India], October 19: Atal Community Innovation Centre (ACIC-VGU), Vivekananda Global University (VGU), Jaipur, has invited applications from eligible startups for *GENESIS Pilot 2.0*, an initiative under the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) Startup Hub. The programme aims to bridge the gap between product validation and commercial deployment by supporting startups in executing real-world pilot projects.
The initiative aims to help eligible startups execute real-world pilots, strengthen product readiness and unlock commercial opportunities
Selected startups may receive *pilot-linked financial support of up to 40 lakh*, subject to eligibility, due diligence and the verified cost of delivering an eligible Pilot Purchase Order (PO) or Work Order (WO).
The initiative is particularly relevant for startups that have secured an eligible pilot engagement from a government department, Public Sector Undertaking (PSU), Fortune 500 company, unicorn or other reputed enterprise.
ACIC-VGU Focuses on Taking Startups from Pilot to Market
GENESIS Pilot 2.0 aims to help startups demonstrate their solutions in real-world environments, address product customisation and deployment requirements, and build a pathway towards repeat orders and commercial growth.
Commenting on the initiative, *Gaurav Sharma, CEO, ACIC-VGU Foundation*, said, "One of the most critical challenges for startups is converting a promising innovation into a market-ready solution that customers are willing to adopt at scale. While many startups develop strong technologies, the journey from a working prototype to successful deployment often requires financial support, industry access and the right incubation ecosystem.
Through GENESIS Pilot 2.0, we aim to help eligible startups bridge this gap by supporting pilot execution and strengthening their readiness for commercialisation. At ACIC-VGU, our focus is on enabling entrepreneurs to validate their solutions in real-world settings, build credibility with potential customers and create sustainable business opportunities. We encourage eligible startups with a strong pilot Purchase Order or Work Order to apply and take the next step towards market adoption."
What Startups Can Access Under GENESIS Pilot 2.0
The programme offers eligible startups the opportunity to access:
- Financial support: Up to 40 lakh per startup, based on the verified cost of the eligible pilot.
- Pilot execution assistance: Support for eligible research and development, product customisation, raw materials, components and manpower engaged in pilot delivery.
- Testing and certification: Eligible expenses related to trials, testing, certifications and licences.
- Incubation support: Mentoring, product-development guidance and access to relevant facilities and ecosystem networks.
- Market connections: Opportunities to connect with potential buyers, industry partners and investors.
Who Can Apply?
ACIC-VGU is inviting applications from startups that meet the prescribed programme criteria, including:
- Incorporated between one and five years ago and based in a Tier 2 or Tier 3 city.
- DPIIT-recognised and operating as a Private Limited Company, with other eligible entity types subject to prescribed conversion requirements.
- At least 51% Indian founder ownership on a fully diluted basis.
- Cumulative revenue of up to 1.5 crore.
- A valid Pilot PO/WO valued between 1 lakh and 1 crore.
- An MVP or working prototype, a viable business plan and at least one full-time founder or co-founder.
- A core product or solution aligned with the prescribed MeitY focus areas.
- Prior government funding of up to 40 lakh and prior private funding of up to 1.5 crore.

Applicants must review the official scheme guidelines for complete eligibility requirements and exclusions. Graduates of a GENESIS EIR cohort may be eligible.
A Valid Pilot Order Is Essential
The programme is designed around the successful execution of an eligible pilot. The proposed engagement must involve the deployment of the startup's own MVP, prototype or product. Resale activities and pure manpower-based services are not eligible.
The Pilot PO/WO should clearly specify the scope of work, deliverables, value, duration and payment terms and must meet the scheme's prescribed validity requirements.
Why Choose ACIC-VGU?
As an implementing incubator, ACIC-VGU Foundation aims to support selected startups through screening, due diligence, mentoring and pilot execution, in line with the programme framework. The Foundation also seeks to facilitate access to relevant facilities, ecosystem partners, prospective buyers and investors.
The initiative is intended to strengthen the connection between startup innovation and real-world adoption, with potential outcomes including successful pilot delivery, commercial contracts, revenue growth, employment generation, intellectual property creation and follow-on funding.
Application Deadline: 30 October 2026
Eligible startups with a strong pilot opportunity are encouraged to apply before the deadline and select *ACIC-VGU Foundation as their preferred incubator*.
