articles.title: India's exports to West Asia recover from US-Iran war shock in April-August; shipments to Africa, ASEAN rise - Livemint
articles.summary: India's exports to West Asia recover from US-Iran war shock in April-August; shipments to Africa, ASEAN rise  Livemint
articles.full_text:
India's exports to West Asia are gradually recovering towards pre-crisis levels after being disrupted by joint military operations launched by the United States and Israel against Iran in late February.
Since then, the conflict has shown little signs of easing, with US President Donald Trump suggesting on Thursday (local time) that Washington could launch another strike on Iran's nuclear facilities, including Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected nuclear site buried deep beneath layers of rock.
India's exports to West Asia stood at $4.2 billion in April, which increased to $5.01 billion in August. It was $6.48 billion in January this year, according to data from the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.
Meanwhile, India's merchandise exports recorded healthy growth across Africa, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and North-East Asia during April-August this fiscal, the data showed.
India's merchandise shipments to Africa rose 47% to $26.19 billion in April-August 2026-27 from $17.83 billion recorded a year earlier.
Africa's share in India's total exports rose to 12.2% during the period under review from 9.7% in the corresponding period last year. Exports to East Africa particularly almost doubled, surging 94% to $8.95 billion.
Shipments to the Southern African Customs Union (SACU) increased 53% to $5.09 billion, and exports to North Africa grew 33% to $4.03 billion.
West Africa recorded a 7% rise in the period to $5.57 billion.
Similarly, shipments to the ASEAN region also recorded a growth of 56% to $23.08 billion, and shipments to North-East Asia rose 37% to $21.03 billion in the April-August period.
Exports to South Asia and other European countries increased 24%.
ASEAN members include Brunei, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, and Vietnam.
Exports of light-duty trucks and medium-duty trucks grew 71% and 67%, respectively, during April-August 2026-27, reflecting strong demand in overseas markets, according to the data.
Optical fibre and cable exports surged 158% to $483 million, while exports of electrical control boards nearly doubled to $303 million. This growth was supported by heightened demand from key markets, including the United States, China, Singapore and Poland.
Overall, India's merchandise exports rose 18.51% to $259.89 billion in April-September 2026-27, compared with $219.30 billion in the corresponding period of the previous fiscal year.
The rise in shipments to various regions during the last quarter reflects the impact of India's efforts to diversify its exports markets. The expansion of India’s trade network comes as rising US tariffs reshape global trade flows.
Since President Donald Trump returned to the White House in January 2025, the US has increased tariffs on several trading partners and product categories.
In response, economies are seeking to diversify their trade relationships and accelerate negotiations with new partners, creating opportunities for countries that can secure preferential market access.
India has accelerated its FTA programme after years of relative caution. During 2025-26, agreements with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), the United Kingdom and Oman entered into force, adding to trade agreements with Australia and the United Arab Emirates that took effect in 2022.
India also signed an FTA with New Zealand and concluded negotiations on a trade agreement with the European Union. New Delhi is pursuing additional partnerships, including with the Eurasian Economic Union, and has sought an agreement with the Gulf Cooperation Council.
(with inputs from PTI)

articles.title: Vietnam signs trade deal with 4 European nations amid US tariff pressure - TheReport.live
articles.summary: Vietnam signs trade deal with 4 European nations amid US tariff pressure  TheReport.live
articles.full_text:
Vietnam has signed a free trade agreement with Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland as it seeks new markets and reduces reliance on major trading partners amid US tariff pressure.
The agreement with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) was signed in Hanoi on Sunday in the presence of Vietnam’s top leader To Lam and representatives of the four European countries.
The deal will eliminate or reduce customs duties on a range of goods, including industrial products, fish and agricultural items.
It also covers trade in services, intellectual property rights, trade remedies and sustainable development.
Vietnam’s government said the agreement would help diversify its import and export markets, strengthen its role in global supply chains and support a rules-based trading system amid global economic uncertainty.
Negotiations began in 2012 but stalled in 2018.
The two sides resumed talks in September last year and concluded negotiations in July.
The agreement comes as US tariffs have disrupted global trade and put pressure on Vietnamese exports to the American market.
Experts say closer ties with EFTA economies could help Vietnam broaden its commercial relationships and move towards higher-value manufacturing.
Trade between EFTA and Vietnam reached 4.8 billion euros ($5.4 billion) last year, according to the association.
EFTA’s main exports to Vietnam included electrical and mechanical machinery, fish and pharmaceutical products.
Vietnam mainly exported machinery, footwear and apparel to the four European countries.
EFTA was established as an alternative to the European Economic Community, the predecessor of the European Union.
Its four members maintain close ties with the EU but are not members of the bloc.

articles.title: No Patriot missiles for Ukraine? Trump holds up transfer as tensions with Zelenskyy rise - The Times of India
articles.summary: No Patriot missiles for Ukraine? Trump holds up transfer as tensions with Zelenskyy rise  The Times of IndiaUkraine war briefing: Zelenskyy claims US deliberately delaying interceptor missile deliveries to Kyiv  The GuardianTrump administration holds up Patriot missiles for Ukraine  The Washington PostExclusive: Ukraine runs out of Patriot interceptor missiles as Zelensky and Trump clash over war  CNNZelensky: Vital supplies from US are delayed  ...
articles.full_text:
The Donald Trump administration has not approved the transfer of Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine from countries that have already acquired the American-made weapons, The Washington Post reported. This comes as tensions between the POTUS and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy deepen. The delay comes as Kyiv faces intensified Russian missile and drone attacks and warns that its stockpile of interceptors is running dangerously low.
The development adds to a growing rift between Washington and Kyiv, with Trump repeatedly criticising Zelenskyy, easing pressure on Moscow and questioning Ukraine's leadership. The strain has also extended to military communications and intelligence support, raising concerns that the shifting US approach could weaken Ukraine's ability to defend itself against Russia.
According to The Washington Post, US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth has neither formally rejected the proposed missile transfers nor completed the necessary steps to approve them. The report, citing a US official and three people familiar with the diplomatic exchanges, said Hegseth had continued to authorise some other forms of US assistance to Ukraine.
Also Read: 
Snow On Fire: Ukraine’s Winter Of Reckoning
Ukraine running low on Patriot interceptors
The United States retains control over the transfer of its weapons to third countries under agreements requiring Washington's approval before they can be passed on to another recipient. This means countries seeking to send their Patriot interceptor missiles to Ukraine need clearance from the US administration.
A Ukrainian official told The Washington Post last week that only a couple of interceptor missiles remained in the country's stockpile. Zelenskyy also told lawmakers during a briefing on Monday that Ukraine had "almost no Patriot interceptors left from the United States" and alleged that the Pentagon was delaying missiles that Kyiv's partners had already paid for.
The shortage comes as Russia continues to target Ukrainian cities and energy infrastructure. Zelenskyy said on Monday that Ukraine had again received no advance warning from partners, including the US, about the latest Russian attacks. He said six people were killed, including a mother and her child, who was just over a year old.
Washington has maintained that it has not stopped providing intelligence to Kyiv. However, separate concerns have emerged over restrictions on Starshield, SpaceX's military-grade satellite communications system, which Ukraine relies on for battlefield communications and drone operations.
Moscow welcomes rift but remains cautious
The growing confrontation has been welcomed by Russian officials, although Moscow remains wary of Trump's unpredictable approach, Reuters reported. The news agency said Kremlin hardliners had seized on the public dispute, but there was little consensus that the tensions had yet translated into a decisive strategic advantage for Russia.
Trump has repeatedly attacked Zelenskyy in recent days and said it was time for Ukraine to get a new president. Russian Security Council deputy chairman Dmitry Medvedev mocked the Ukrainian leader on Telegram, while Kremlin economic envoy Kirill Dmitriev argued that Zelenskyy's criticism of Trump would have significant consequences.
The tensions have coincided with Trump's decision to ease certain restrictions affecting Russian fuel supplies and refrain from imposing additional sanctions on buyers of Russian oil. However, some Russian commentators have questioned whether these moves would deliver substantial benefits to Moscow, with one pro-Kremlin lawmaker suggesting that Trump's decisions were driven largely by domestic political considerations ahead of the US congressional midterm elections.

articles.title: Prolonged European unrest may add pressure on Bangladesh’s exports - Daily Bonik Barta
articles.summary: Prolonged European unrest may add pressure on Bangladesh’s exports  Daily Bonik Barta
articles.full_text:
Violent protests driven by discontent over rising living costs, the quality of public services and conditions in educational institutions have spread across France. On October 17, clashes between protesters and police, looting and arson were reported in Paris, Lyon, Marseille, Limoges and other cities. Limoges’s 150-year-old historic city hall was burned down.
On the same day, a protest in Milan against rising living costs and an anti-war demonstration turned violent. Clashes, looting and arson broke out in the city centre, leaving Piazza del Duomo and the luxury shops beside it, normally busy with shoppers and tourists, empty.
Belgium and Portugal have also seen protests against rising living costs.
Europe is one of the main markets for Bangladeshi garment exports, with nearly half of Bangladesh’s total ready-made garment exports going to the EU market.
Exporters fear that prolonged political and social unrest in various European countries and any shift in European consumers’ spending and purchasing behaviour could could hit those exports.
Stakeholders say demand for garments in the European market has long been growing slowly. Fresh uncertainty could put the country’s garment exports under pressure. Observers believe that alongside conditions in Europe, Bangladesh’s own competitiveness will also matter in managing that risk.
Export-sector stakeholders, however, say it is not yet possible to say how long the unrest in Europe will last or how it will affect import demand.
Mahmud Hasan Khan, president of the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA), told Bonik Barta: “Business and trade are directly linked to law and order. Tourists are important buyers in various European countries. If unrest disrupts tourism and the normal movement of people, it could affect product sales. That will create challenges for Bangladeshi exporters as well, and there is a risk of loss.”
EU countries took 49.25 percent of Bangladesh’s total garment exports in the 2025–26 fiscal year, according to Export Promotion Bureau (EPB) figures. Shipments to the bloc were worth $19.06 billion, 3.31 percent less than in the previous year.
Among the EU’s major markets, Germany accounted for 11.32 percent of Bangladesh’s total garment exports, followed by Spain on 9.31 percent, the Netherlands 5.61 percent, France 5.09 percent and Italy 3.67 percent.
Year on year, exports fell 11.50 percent to Germany, 8.74 percent to France and 7.78 percent to Italy. Recent political and social unrest in these large European markets has compounded an export downturn already underway, putting Bangladeshi garment exporters under pressure on two fronts.
The picture in the first quarter of the current 2026–27 fiscal year is somewhat different. EPB data show ready-made garment exports to the EU reached $4.90 billion between July and September, up 3.33 percent on the same period a year earlier.
RMG exports to Spain rose 13.73 percent in the first quarter, the Netherlands 9.02 percent, Poland 5.77 percent and Sweden 14.43 percent.
By contrast, exports to France fell by 4.91 percent, Italy by 5.82 percent and Germany by 0.15 percent. Exports may be growing overall, but several important EU markets remain in decline, and France and Italy, two of those markets, are where the violence is now playing out.
MS Dyeing Printing and Finishing Ltd is one of the largest exporters of Bangladeshi garments to Europe. Its managing director, Md Mamunur Rashid, said the company was already feeling the effects.
He told Bonik Barta: “We’ve comparatively fewer orders now, lower than what we would normally have. The current unrest is new but orders were already down before it because of the slump. Our factory hasn’t been in a situation like this in recent years.”
BGMEA and BKMEA officials say it is not yet possible to establish separately how much of the decline in orders is specifically attributable to the unrest. They fear, however, that a prolonged crisis could inflict serious damage on the export sector.
Large European buyers are already adjusting their sourcing. Industry figures say international brands including H&M, Inditex and Primark are shifting part of their orders out of Bangladesh to India, Egypt and other destinations.
Industry figures say buyers are seeking to reduce reliance on any single country and diversify their production and sourcing, while weighing up purchase prices, delivery times and production costs.
Bangladeshi exporters say slower global demand and buyers’ efforts to save on costs are behind the shift, alongside Bangladesh’s production costs and uncertain energy supply. Competitor countries, including India, manufacture at comparatively lower cost, while the prospect of greater trade benefits in future is also influencing how orders are distributed.
Industrialists believe the unrest in Europe could now significantly affect buyers’ purchasing behaviour.
Nuria Lopez, chairperson of the European Union Chamber of Commerce in Bangladesh (EuroCham), says she is more concerned about Bangladesh’s internal competitiveness than about the potential impact of the European unrest.
“The current unrest in Europe could affect Bangladesh’s exports, but it would not affect Bangladesh alone; it could have implications for businesses and trade across the world,” she told Bonik Barta.
She added: “Political polarisation, upcoming elections in several countries, the high cost of living and pressure on energy markets amid the Iran war have created global uncertainty.”
For Bangladesh’s garment exports, her main concern is “domestic competitiveness”, particularly gas and electricity shortages, labour unrest, wage disputes and the lack of stability in the business environment.
“Bangladesh needs to send a strong message of stability to investors and buyers. It is also important to begin discussions on a free trade agreement (FTA) with the European Union, as this would demonstrate that Europe views Bangladesh as an important trading partner,” Lopez said.
“At the same time, Bangladesh must ensure law and order, the security of export operations and the modernisation of its logistics sector,” she added.
Lopez stressed that the growing competitiveness of India is another issue Bangladesh needs to watch closely, adding that there was a risk that sourcing orders, particularly for cotton-related products, could shift from Bangladesh to India.
“If the unrest in Europe continues for an extended period, its implications will need to be reassessed. However, at this stage, I am not particularly concerned about the impact of the current unrest in Europe on trade between Europe and Bangladesh. Addressing Bangladesh’s domestic challenges is far more important at this point,” the EuroCham chairperson said.
The strain is visible in EU import data as well. Eurostat figures show that the EU’s garment imports fell 3.83 percent between January and August 2025.
Over the same eight months, the value of imports from Bangladesh dropped from €13.50 billion to €11.92 billion, a fall of 11.67 percent, nearly three times the decline in the EU’s total garment imports.
Prolonged instability in Europe would be a major worry for Bangladesh’s exports, said Mohammad Hatem, president of the knitwear manufacturers’ and exporters’ group BKMEA. “Sales in the European market have already fallen, and the impact of the global economic downturn has reached Bangladesh,” he told Bonik Barta.
Bangladesh would not be the only country to see garment exports fall, said Dr Mohammad Abdur Razzaque, chairman of the research group Research and Policy Integration for Development (RAPID).
“Everyone who exports garments to the EU could be affected,” he told Bonik Barta. “Oil prices are adding to that. And Europe’s gas demand and prices may rise in winter. Weighing up inflationary pressure and the present unrest, I think trade with Europe will contract in the coming days.”
Asked why the risk was greater for Bangladesh, Razzaque said: “The concern is greater for Bangladesh because of the concentration of our markets. We haven’t built any substantial market outside the EU.”
Export Promotion Bureau vice-chairman Mohammad Hasan Arif does not believe the European unrest should be treated directly as a market crisis. Such unrest is mainly an expression of social and economic discontent, and there is no certainty that imports fall whenever a country becomes unstable, he noted, adding that Bangladesh’s exports grew in the first quarter of the current fiscal year.
“If prolonged, it is genuinely impossible to predict which way things will go,” he said. “Crises of this kind in business and trade will keep coming. Our exporters have to learn to deal with them and to stay prepared for potential crises at all times.”

articles.title: India's Russia crude imports fell 12% in September, Trump waiver may revive buying - Dailyhunt
articles.summary: India's Russia crude imports fell 12% in September, Trump waiver may revive buying  Dailyhunt
articles.full_text:
India's import of Russian crude fell 12 percent from the previous month to €3.6 billion ($4.04 billion) in September, data from Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air (CREA), a Helsinki-based think-tank, shows.
The country, however, remained the second-largest buyer of Russian barrels.
Indian refiners pulled back purchases after the US threatened to impose up to 100 percent tariffs on countries buying energy from Moscow, analysts say.
"Russian crude imports fell at all three of India's largest importing refineries including Vadinar (down 8 percent month-on-month), Jamnagar (down 27 percent), and Paradip (down 21 percent). Despite the decline, Vadinar overtook Jamnagar as India's largest importer of Russian crude," CREA said.
The country was also the second-largest buyer of Russian fossil fuels in September, importing a total of €4.1 billion of hydrocarbons against €4.8 billion ($5.39 billion) in August.
Crude constituted 88 percent of Russian purchases, totalling €3.6 billion. Coal valued at €309 million ($347.12 million) and oil products at €161 million ($180.86 million) constituted the remainder of the Russian imports during the month.
However, the average price of Russia's Urals-grade crude rose by 32 percent from August to $90.7 a barrel. According to CERA, it is highest monthly average since April and more than double the EU and UK price cap of $44.1.
US tariff waiver to ease pressure
On October 17, US President Donald Trump waived sanctions, restrictions and duties under a law targeting Russia and Iran, citing American national interests.
Analysts see India continuing the purchase of Russian oil with imports expected to remain robust at 1.8-1.9 million barrels a day, commodity analytics firm Kpler has said.
"For India, the immediate relief matters. Exporters escape a potentially severe tariff shock, while oil buyers gain breathing space," said Ajay Srivastava, founder, Global Trade Research Initiative.
India imports over 88 percent of its oil requirements. Capitalising on heavy discounts on Urals crude, the country has emerged as a top buyer of Russian oil since the outbreak of the Russia-Ukraine war in 2022.
Russia's share of India's oil imports, however, fell from 51 percent in July to 44 percent in August as India bought more from the US, despite higher prices and from the UAE amidst tariff threat.
While Indian refiners may continue Russian oil imports, experts caution that the tariff threat can return and become leverage for concessions in trade negotiations.
"India needs to protect energy security and buy oil on commercial terms, prepare for renewed US tariff pressure, and judge any trade deal by the durable, reciprocal benefits it delivers," Srivastava said.

articles.title: Indian IT giants' H-1B visa registrations fall amid Trump's crackdown; Infosys, Cognizant, TCS report fewer entries - Livemint
articles.summary: Indian IT giants' H-1B visa registrations fall amid Trump's crackdown; Infosys, Cognizant, TCS report fewer entries  Livemint
articles.full_text:
As US President Donald Trump's administration tightens immigration policies, including a $100,000 fee for certain new H-1B applications and a wage-weighted selection system introduced for fiscal year 2027, H-1B registrations by major IT companies such as Cognizant, Infosys and Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) have dropped in the FY2027 lottery.
According to data in a Congressional Research Service (CRS) report published on 14 October, Cognizant submitted 100% fewer registrations than in the previous year, while Infosys' registrations declined by 91% and TCS's plunged by 95%.
The report, "H-1B Executive Actions in 2026", comes at a time when the Trump administration has announced changes to H-1B visa selection and fees as the government seeks to prioritise higher-paid workers and address what it calls abuse of the programme.
According to data from US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS), the company-level figures highlight the scale of the decline. Infosys submitted 759 registrations for FY2027, down from 8,886 in FY2026, while TCS’s total declined to 284 from 5,955. Cognizant recorded no registrations, compared with 3,752 the previous year.
A Federal Register publication dated 23 September 2026 also highlighted the decline, reporting that combined H-1B registrations by the largest IT staffing and outsourcing firms fell by roughly 92%, from 24,946 to 2,055.
The figures cover entries in the annual H-1B cap selection process, rather than the companies’ total H-1B workforce. They do not indicate that current visa holders have lost their immigration status.
According to the CRS report, the wage-weighted selection system, introduced by the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) in February this year, was used for the FY2027 H-1B lottery. The fiscal year began this month. The weighted selection process is designed to favour highly skilled and higher-paid workers.
Employers have also faced a $100,000 fee introduced last September for certain new H-1B workers entering the US from abroad. In the first eight months after it took effect, initial H-1B petitions requesting consular processing from employers exempt from the annual visa cap fell by 91% compared with the same period a year earlier.
According to a Hindustan Times report, the sharp decline in registrations may indicate that Indian IT firms are changing how they staff US projects, potentially placing greater reliance on workers already in the country, visa extensions, transfers and local recruitment. Infosys, TCS and Cognizant reduced fresh registrations against a backdrop of rising costs and changes to the H-1B selection process.
While the registration figures alone cannot establish the number of jobs lost or how many Indian professionals will ultimately be able to work in the US, they indicate a substantial decline in fresh lottery registrations by some of the largest IT companies employing Indian professionals, despite Indians accounting for the biggest share of H-1B visa holders in the US.

articles.title: NSAM 2.0: Supporting Startup India and propelling GDP - Organiser
articles.summary: NSAM 2.0: Supporting Startup India and propelling GDP  Organiser
articles.full_text:
More than four years after the National Strategy for Additive Manufacturing (NSAM) was launched in February 2022, the government data tells a sharper story of success. Over 1,54,000 individuals have been trained, 56 start-ups have been backed and 65 India-specific technologies have been developed.
Data released by the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), NSAM’s show a strategy running well ahead of target in some respects and still catching up in others. A close reading of these data is the clearest way to judge how India’n additive manufacturing (AM) mission is actually performing and where its next phase NSAM 2.0 will need to focus its energy.
The roadmap itself set out six measurable commitments with a 5 percent share of the global AM market, nearly US$1 billion added to India’s GDP, 50 India-specific AM technologies, 100 new AM start-ups, a lakh newly skilled workers and capability built across 10 manufacturing sectors.
Four years on have hard progress figures attached to them in the public record, one has strong indirect evidence and two remain without a disclosed update. That pattern of disclosure is itself a data point worth reading carefully.
The skilling number that beats its own target
NSAM roadmap set a target of training one lakh new skilled workers for the AM workforce. The reported figure over 1,54,000 individuals trained, it is a target exceeded by roughly 54,000 people or 54 percent above plan and that overshoot is no accident of counting.
It reflects a funnel built deliberately into the strategy. At the school level, Atal Tinkering Labs equipped with 3D printers, robotics and Internet of Things kits each backed by a ₹20-lakh grant and built into 1,200 to 1,500 square foot innovation spaces expose students from Grade VI to Grade XII to AM fundamentals years before they enter a workforce.
Layered on top are the seven specialised Development and Deployment Centres, which combine research with hands-on technology access and skilling. When training infrastructure is put in place early and widely, the resulting numbers tend to outrun paper targets a pattern worth watching as NSAM 2.0 is conceptualised.
Start-ups and technologies
Not every metric tells the same success story and an honest data read has to hold both halves together. The 65 India specific technologies developed spanning materials, machines, processes and software run well past the roadmap goal, the clearest sign that India’s AM research base is maturing faster than planned.
Start-up creation tells a different story where the enterprise layer of the ecosystem is running at roughly half the pace of its technology-development layer. It suggests NSAM has been more effective at generating deep technology than at converting that technology into commercial ventures at scale precisely the gap that NSAM 2.0 emphasis on Intellectual Property Rights generation and globally competitive commercialisation appears designed to close.
Sector Coverage: Eight named, two still unaccounted
NSAM roadmap commits to building AM capability across 10 existing and emerging manufacturing sectors. Tallying the sectors explicitly named in the government’s own account of progress gives a reasonably precise picture: aerospace and space (Agnikul Cosmos’s AM-printed rocket engine), defence (army dwellings and precast structures in Ladakh), healthcare (silk implants, bioceramic bone grafts), electronics (AM-printed batteries, antennas, capacitors and IISc’s globally first photonic circuit blocks), construction (2,500 square foot homes in under 30 days), energy (concrete-based supercapacitors for solar storage), food processing and photonics.
That totals eight distinct sectors with activity 80 percent of the ten-sector target, thus leaving two where the current release offers no specific evidence yet. NSAM institutional backbone is a network of seven Development and Deployment Centres, each assigned a distinct technological mandate and spread across seven different states.
The spread is deliberately non-metropolitan in places Mandi and Mehsana sit alongside Hyderabad and Bengaluru by spreading AM infrastructure beyond India’s traditional technology hubs rather than concentrating it in one or two cities.
The market arithmetic
The government’s own backgrounder frames India’s opportunity against two external numbers: a global AM machines market projected to reach US$149 billion by 2035 and an AM-electronics supply chain expected to grow from US$18 billion to US$112 billion, a roughly 6.2-fold expansion.
Reading NSAM’s stated ambition of a 5 percent global market share against that US$149 billion figure implies a prize in the range of US$7.4 billion for India once the market matures well above the strategy’s own near-term target of adding nearly US$1 billion to GDP.
The gap between the near-term GDP target and the long-term market-share ambition is itself informative: it signals NSAM’s current numbers represent an early, foundational phase, with the larger payoff due only once start-up creation and commercialisation catch up to where technology development already stands.
Independent trackers such as the Wohlers Report size the broader global AM industry at roughly US$21.9 billion for 2024 with a narrower measure than the government’s machines-focused projection, but one confirming the same trend where AM is a fast-expanding industry, and India’s targets are calibrated to a market that will look very different in 2035.
The platforms carrying the numbers forward
Two dated events in the record show how the ecosystem is being convened, and the cadence matters as much as the content. The National Additive Manufacturing Symposium (NAMS) held its second edition on 13 March 2026 in New Delhi, bringing policymakers, scientists, start-ups and academia onto one platform, exchanging MoUs and launching new AM products while covering NSAM 2.0, defence adoption and MeitY-supported R&D centres in its panel discussions.
Seven months later, the Emerging Science, Technology and Innovation Conclave (ESTIC-2026) is set to convene at Bharat Mandapam, Pragati Maidan, from 27 to 29 October 2026, organised by the Council of Scientific & Industrial Research across 12 thematic areas, with Additive Manufacturing listed among the frontier technologies on its agenda.
Two national scale AM convenings within a single calendar year is itself a measurable signal of institutional momentum a cadence that was not part of the original NSAM roadmap but has clearly become part of how the strategy is now being executed.
What the data suggests next
Put together, NSAM numbers describe a strategy that has outperformed on research depth and workforce creation, kept pace on sectoral spread, and lagged on converting technology into start-ups and finished products.
For NSAM 2.0, now being conceptualised with an explicit focus on Intellectual Property Rights generation, digital integration and commercialisation, the data points to where the next phase of effort needs to concentrate not on generating more India-specific technologies, where the strategy is already 30 percent ahead of plan, but on the harder task of turning that technological base into the 100 start-ups with 500 products and 5 percent global market share that remain the mission unmet benchmarks.

articles.title: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow - BBC
articles.summary: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow  BBCIran war updates: Tankers reported hit in Hormuz; drones downed near Riyadh  Al JazeeraOil Tanker On 'Unauthorised Route' Hits Mine In Hormuz, Catches Fire  NDTV'War booty': Cheap iPhone 18s advertised in Tehran after Hormuz shipwreck, claims report  The Times of IndiaIran's military says oil tanker on fire in Gulf of Oman  The Hindu
articles.full_text:
The number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows.
Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks.
Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks.
As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests.
BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported.
Experts say Tehran has been attacking ships in an effort to assert greater control over the waterway as the US military has increased the number of tankers it is shepherding through the south of the strait to evade Iranian strikes.
Iran is also carrying out more attacks on vessels further away from the Strait of Hormuz, according to experts.
The US military's Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, posted on social media that despite the attacks "commercial traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with co-ordinated protection from US forces and regional partners".
Two crew missing after one of Sunday's attacks
The aftermath of one of Sunday's six reported attacks was captured in verified footage showing the Nicaragua-flagged tanker Petro Dolphin on fire, as filmed by the crew on a smaller boat nearby.
The vessel was struck by a drone close to the Sohar Anchorage, Oman, more than 250km (150 miles) from the strait, according to the maritime intelligence firm Vanguard.
Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued but two are still missing, the Forward Seamen's Union of India said.
Attacks have continued this week with the container ship GFS Pride sinking after a strike by an unknown projectile in the strait on Tuesday. Twenty-one crew were safely evacuated.
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) published footage of what appeared to be the same ship sinking. It said the vessel was carrying "2,500 containers of contraband" and had taken an "unauthorised route".
Oil shipments stall
Middle East oil exports have slowed as the number of ship strikes has risen.
About 12.6 million barrels per day went through the strait on 13 October, below the 15 million reported at the end of September, data from trade intelligence firm Kpler shows. This compares with a pre-war baseline of some 17 million barrels per day.
The recent increase in attacks comes as US Navy data indicates the number of vessels given assistance to navigate the Strait of Hormuz during the first 10 days of October was up 85% compared with the same period in August.
Most of the oil being shipped from Gulf Arab states recently has been carried using a "shuttle" system where a fleet of tankers load up and sail through the strait before transferring their cargo to larger tankers in the Gulf of Oman.
These shuttle ships use a route close to Oman's coastline. Iran says this is "unauthorised" and insist vessels take an alternative route closer to its own shore.
So-called assisted transits were a key factor in helping drive oil flows from the Middle East back towards pre-war levels in September. This does not include Iranian exports which have completely stalled as a result of the US blockade of Iranian ports and ships.
Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, said Iran has "evolved its strategy" in response to this loosening of its control over the strait and has been carrying out "near daily or multiple attacks every single day".
"The aim here is to stop the ships going through and to deter others," he added.
The IRGC's navy has said strikes would not be "limited to the Strait of Hormuz" and later announced a "new deployment formation" across the region, according to state media.
Martin Kelly told BBC Verify that Iran is widening its attacks and targeting ships near the coast of Gulf Arab states and in the Gulf of Oman.
A tanker was struck by multiple projectiles north of Qatar on Thursday 8 October, more than 500km (310 miles) from the strait, resulting in multiple reported casualties, according to Vanguard.
Another tanker was attacked close to the UAE town of Al-Jazirah al-Hamra on Friday 9 October, Vanguard said.
Verified footage later showed crew members running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rose over the ship.
Additional reporting by Becky Dale
Graphics by Tom Shiel and Mark Edwards

articles.title: India GDP Growth Forecast Raised to 7% for FY27 and FY28 - Business Viewpoint Magazine
articles.summary: India GDP Growth Forecast Raised to 7% for FY27 and FY28  Business Viewpoint Magazine
articles.full_text:
Key takeaways:
- The IMF projects India’s economy to grow 7% in FY27 and FY28.
- Global economic growth is forecast to reach 3.1% in 2026.
- India’s inflation could reach 5% in FY27 before easing in FY28.
The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has raised the India GDP growth forecast to 7% for FY27 and FY28, citing resilient domestic demand, services activity, and favourable demographic trends. The revised outlook places India’s projected growth above the global economy’s expected expansion of 3.1% in 2026. For Indian entrepreneurs and business owners, the estimates offer a view of expected economic activity, while inflation and energy costs remain important factors.
India’s growth outlook strengthens against global trends
In its October 2026 World Economic Outlook, the IMF raised its growth estimate for India in FY27 to 7%, up from 6.4% projected in July. It also revised its FY28 forecast upwards to 7% from 6.7%.
The IMF identified an expanding domestic market, favourable demographic trends, and continued structural reforms as factors supporting India’s growth potential. Domestic consumption and services activity have also helped the economy maintain momentum despite uncertainty in international markets.
The Fund expects the global economy to grow by 3.1% in 2026, slightly above its July estimate of 3%. Global growth stood at 3.5% in 2025. For 2027, the IMF projects growth of 3.4%, unchanged from its previous forecast.
India’s projected growth rate is more than twice the expected global rate for 2026. The figures reflect different growth paths across economies, with domestic demand and services supporting India’s outlook.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) has projected growth of 7.1% for FY27, slightly above the IMF’s India GDP growth forecast of 7%.
For businesses, the India GDP growth forecast provides context for planning around consumer demand, operating capacity, and investment. However, actual results will depend on conditions across individual industries and changes in domestic and international markets.
Oil prices and inflation remain key economic risks
Higher crude oil prices remain a potential source of pressure for India, which relies heavily on imports to meet its energy needs.
The IMF’s October outlook assumes an average crude oil price of $95.74 per barrel in 2026, an increase of around 41% from 2025. It expects the average to fall to $87.39 per barrel in 2027.
Sustained high oil prices could raise India’s import bill and put pressure on its current account balance. Higher energy costs can also increase transport, manufacturing, and other operating expenses for businesses. If companies pass these costs on to consumers, household purchasing power may come under pressure.
The IMF expects India’s consumer inflation to reach 5% in FY27 before easing to 4.4% in FY28. It also projects the current account deficit to reach 1.5% of gross domestic product in FY27.
Globally, inflation is expected to reach 4.7% in 2026 before moderating to 4.1% in 2027. Higher energy and food prices are among the factors behind the projection.
The IMF also noted that investment linked to artificial intelligence has supported economic activity in some parts of the world, although the benefits have varied across economies. Energy price increases and uncertainty in international markets remain risks to the global outlook.
India’s revised forecast points to continued economic expansion over the next 2 fiscal years. The pace of growth will also depend on domestic spending, inflation, energy prices, and global trade and investment conditions.

articles.summary: BRICS and Pakistan: New Opportunities for Growth  The Daily CPEC

BRICS and Pakistan have a growing relevance to discussions about economic diversification, development finance and long-term investment. As Pakistan faces substantial external financing requirements and seeks funding for infrastructure, energy and industrial development, engagement with BRICS-linked institutions could widen its options. However, access to financing is not automatic. It will depend on institutional arrangements, the quality of proposed projects and Pakistan’s ability to turn investment into sustainable economic growth.
For Islamabad, the opportunity lies in diversifying its economic partnerships rather than replacing existing lenders. With substantial external financing requirements and pressure to maintain economic stability, Pakistan needs capital that strengthens productive capacity, expands exports and supports long-term growth. BRICS could become one part of that strategy, provided diplomatic engagement translates into practical economic outcomes.
BRICS and Pakistan’s Development Finance Challenge
Pakistan’s external financing requirements remain substantial. The International Monetary Fund’s April 2026 report projected gross external financing requirements of approximately US$18.8 billion for 2026–27 and US$29.9 billion for 2028–29. These estimates cover external obligations and financing needs, including debt repayments and projected current-account pressures. They are projections, not amounts Pakistan must necessarily borrow from a single lender. These projections are detailed in the IMF’s April 2026 country report.
The figures underline why Pakistan needs a broad network of financial partners. Multilateral institutions, bilateral lenders, private investors and export-generating businesses all have roles to play. Dependence on a narrow range of financing sources can leave the economy exposed when borrowing conditions tighten or repayments fall due.
BRICS-related institutions could potentially widen the channels available for development projects. However, development finance cannot automatically resolve immediate foreign-exchange shortages or eliminate existing debt. Its longer-term contribution would be to support investments that improve productivity and strengthen Pakistan’s capacity to earn foreign exchange.
The New Development Bank: A Potential Financing Channel
The New Development Bank (NDB), established in 2015 by Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, is a multilateral development bank created to mobilise resources for infrastructure and sustainable development.
For BRICS and Pakistan, the New Development Bank offers a potential avenue for diversifying development finance, subject to the institution’s membership and financing requirements.
The bank finances projects across areas such as clean energy, transport, water management, urban development and digital infrastructure. During its first decade, it approved approximately US$43 billion across 140 projects on a gross basis. At 31 December 2025, its portfolio comprised 115 projects with US$35.6 billion in NDB financing, after accounting for cancellations and fully repaid loans. The bank’s infrastructure-financing portfolio illustrates the range of development projects it supports.
These figures demonstrate that the NDB has developed into an operating development-finance institution. They do not, however, mean that Pakistan can automatically access its resources.
BRICS membership and NDB membership are separate processes. The bank has its own admission arrangements, and financing decisions depend on eligibility, institutional approvals and individual project assessments. Pakistan’s potential access should therefore be treated as a possibility requiring confirmation, not an established entitlement. The distinction is reflected in the New Development Bank’s membership and admission arrangements.
What BRICS Could Mean for Pakistan’s Economy
Pakistan faces infrastructure and investment needs across energy, transport, water management, urban services and climate resilience. It also needs capital for industrial zones, digital connectivity, renewable energy and logistics.
These sectors require long-term financing that can be difficult to secure through commercial borrowing alone. If Pakistan becomes eligible for NDB support, projects in these areas could potentially fit the bank’s development mandate.
Potential areas of cooperation include:
- Renewable-energy generation and electricity transmission.
- Urban water, sanitation and public transport.
- Climate-resilient infrastructure.
- Digital networks and logistics.
- Industrial infrastructure that supports manufacturing and exports.
The key consideration is project quality, not the political symbolism of joining a new grouping. Projects need realistic cost estimates, transparent procurement, credible repayment or revenue plans and measurable development benefits.
Pakistan would also need to compare any proposed financing with options available from existing development banks and bilateral partners. New finance is valuable when it improves the country’s choices, not simply when it adds another borrowing channel.
Local-Currency Financing and Exchange-Rate Risks
Local-currency financing is another area worth watching. The NDB has identified the use of local currencies as a strategic priority, alongside efforts to diversify its funding and lending arrangements.
For Pakistan, this issue has direct economic significance. When an infrastructure loan is denominated in a foreign currency but project revenues are earned in rupees, depreciation can increase the domestic cost of servicing the debt. That mismatch can strain project finances and, where the government bears the risk, public budgets.
Financing in local currency could reduce some of this exposure. However, it would not automatically make borrowing cheaper or eliminate currency risks. The availability and cost of such arrangements depend on capital-market depth, investor confidence, inflation, interest rates and financial regulation.
Pakistan would need stronger domestic financial markets and credible macroeconomic management to benefit from alternative financing instruments. The relevant questions are whether a loan is affordable, whether its repayment structure is sustainable and whether the project can generate sufficient economic value.
BRICS, Pakistan and the Search for Alternative Finance
BRICS-related financing could potentially complement Pakistan-China cooperation under the China-Pakistan Economic Corridor (CPEC). The corridor has focused on energy, transport and connectivity, while CPEC 2.0 places greater emphasis on industrial cooperation, agriculture, technology, minerals and business-to-business investment.
These sectors require capital that supports productive activity, not infrastructure construction alone. Industrial facilities, logistics networks and renewable-energy projects can contribute to growth when they operate efficiently, attract businesses and generate sustainable returns.
The NDB could provide an additional multilateral channel for eligible projects if Pakistan meets the bank’s requirements. This would not mean replacing Chinese investment or existing development partners. Instead, Pakistan could seek a broader mix of financing sources where projects qualify and where institutions can contribute effectively.
A CPEC-linked project would not automatically qualify for NDB funding. Each proposal would need to satisfy the relevant institution’s financing criteria, safeguards and approval procedures. Pakistan’s priority should be to prepare projects that are commercially credible and deliver clear benefits for the wider economy.
Why BRICS Cannot Replace the IMF
Debates about BRICS sometimes centre on reducing dependence on Western-led financial institutions. Diversifying financial partnerships may offer strategic advantages, but the economic functions of these institutions differ.
The IMF provides balance-of-payments support and works with governments on economic stabilisation programmes. Development banks such as the NDB primarily finance longer-term infrastructure and sustainable-development projects. They are not interchangeable sources of funding.
Pakistan should therefore not treat BRICS as a substitute for the IMF. Stabilisation arrangements, development lending, private investment and domestic economic reform address different parts of the country’s financial challenge.
A more realistic strategy would maintain access to necessary stabilisation support while expanding investment partnerships and improving the conditions for business growth. This includes predictable regulations, stronger public institutions, competitive exports and more effective management of public debt.
Project Preparation Will Determine the Outcome
Access to finance is only one part of the development challenge. Countries must also prepare projects that lenders can assess and implement effectively.
Development institutions examine financial viability, procurement arrangements, environmental and social safeguards, implementation capacity and repayment prospects. Weak proposals can delay investment even when funding is available.
Pakistan would benefit from stronger coordination between federal and provincial agencies, better project appraisal and clearer implementation timelines. Investors also need confidence that regulations will remain predictable and approved projects will not face avoidable administrative delays.
The same principle applies to private capital. Investment announcements do not guarantee construction, commercial operation or employment. Investors need credible revenue models, transparent rules and a clear understanding of project risks. Stronger project preparation could therefore improve Pakistan’s ability to attract finance from the NDB and other development institutions alike.

articles.title: Marco Rubio In India Today: What’s On The Agenda As Trade Deal Talks Near Finish Line - Times Now
articles.summary: Marco Rubio In India Today: What’s On The Agenda As Trade Deal Talks Near Finish Line  Times Now
articles.full_text:
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio begins a three-day visit to India on Tuesday, with trade, tariffs, defence cooperation and the West Asia crisis expected to feature prominently in discussions between the two countries.
Rubio’s second visit to India this year comes at a time when bilateral ties remain strained over trade and other policy issues. During his previous visit in May, he met Prime Minister Narendra Modi and External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar and attended a Quad foreign ministers’ meeting.
According to the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), Rubio is scheduled to arrive at Mumbai’s Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj International Airport at 2:15 pm on Tuesday. He is expected to meet Jaishankar later in the day to discuss ways to strengthen the India-US Comprehensive Global Strategic Partnership.
The two sides are expected to discuss energy, trade and investment, defence, critical and emerging technologies, and other areas of mutual interest.
"Discussions are expected to cover key areas of bilateral cooperation, including energy, trade and investment, defence, critical and emerging technologies, and other areas of mutual interest," MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said last week.
26/11 tribute, US independence anniversary on agenda
During his Mumbai visit, Rubio is scheduled to lay a wreath at the Taj memorial to honour the victims of the November 26, 2008, Mumbai terror attacks. The attacks killed more than 160 people, including six American citizens.
He will also attend a reception marking the 250th anniversary of US independence.
Rubio will travel to Jamnagar in Gujarat on Wednesday as part of his three-day India tour.
India-US trade deal: Are both sides nearing an agreement?
The proposed bilateral trade agreement is expected to be a key focus of Rubio’s discussions with Indian officials, with both countries seeking to resolve differences over tariffs and market access.
Ahead of his visit, Rubio said in Uzbekistan that Washington was close to finalising the trade agreement with New Delhi. He also indicated that the proposed deal could be a factor in decisions on tariff waivers related to India’s purchases of Russian oil.
"We're trying to finalise the trade deal with India right now. We're very close to doing that. So that's one of the things we take into consideration when the President makes a decision about national security waivers and things of that nature," Rubio said.
India and the US have been negotiating the proposed trade pact since early 2025. The discussions aim to address tariff-related differences, remove non-tariff barriers and improve market access for businesses in both countries.
India is seeking more favourable tariff rates for its goods in the US market compared with those offered to competing countries.
Jaishankar recently said the negotiations were approaching a "landing point", raising expectations that the two sides could make progress towards an agreement.
Relations between New Delhi and Washington have faced several challenges over the past year.
Ties deteriorated after the US imposed punitive tariffs on Indian goods and President Donald Trump claimed a role in de-escalating the India-Pakistan military clashes in May 2025. The remarks drew a sharp reaction from Indian officials.
Differences over US immigration policies and an increase in H-1B visa fees have added to the concerns, particularly among Indian professionals and technology companies.
Relations came under further pressure after Washington moved to restrict a key green-card processing programme affecting major global and Indian IT companies, including Tata Consultancy Services and Wipro.
Against this backdrop, Rubio’s visit offers an opportunity for both countries to sustain high-level engagement and work towards resolving differences over trade and other bilateral issues.
"The visit will provide an opportunity to sustain the high-level engagement between the two countries and advance our shared priorities," Jaiswal had said.

articles.full_text:
India’s infrastructure sector continued to expand across roads, aviation, telecommunications, ports, power and railways, according to the latest quarterly update of the PAIMANA Performance Monitoring Dashboard released by the Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI).
The dashboard records progress across key infrastructure indicators, offering a consolidated picture of capacity expansion, utilisation, connectivity and service delivery. Among the major developments, National Highway projects awarded during the first six months of the current financial year increased sharply, while air cargo volumes and electronic toll collection also registered growth.
The latest update expands the dashboard to 184 indicators, including 21 newly added indicators. Quarterly data has been updated for 41 indicators covering power, civil aviation, ports, shipping and waterways, and road transport and highways.
Launched on April 16, 2026, the PAIMANA dashboard provides a unified digital platform to monitor infrastructure performance and support evidence-based policymaking. MoSPI said the platform would continue to be updated quarterly to improve transparency and make official infrastructure statistics more accessible.
Highway project awards Rise 62.9 percent
The road transport and highways sector recorded one of the strongest increases in the latest dashboard update. A total of 2,236.3 kilometres of National Highway projects were awarded during April-September 2026-27, marking a year-on-year increase of 62.9 percent.
The rise in project awards indicates an expansion in the pipeline of highway infrastructure projects. However, the length of projects awarded should be distinguished from the length of highways completed or opened to traffic. The dashboard figure relates to projects awarded during the period.
Electronic toll collection also recorded substantial growth. Transactions reached 225.2 crore during April-September, an increase of 24.1 percent compared with the corresponding period a year earlier.
The value of electronic toll collection stood at Rs 36,994.5 crore, registering year-on-year growth of 11.7 percent.
The increase in toll transactions reflects greater use of electronic payment systems across the highway network. The difference between transaction growth and the increase in collection value also indicates that the two indicators are moving at different rates, although the figures alone do not establish the reasons for this difference.
Together, the highway and toll data provide an indication of activity across road infrastructure and its associated payment systems.
Optical fibre network expands across India
Telecommunications connectivity also registered progress, with the cumulative optical fibre cable network reaching 7,52,113 kilometres by August 2026.
An additional 29,256 kilometres of optical fibre cable were added between April and August, strengthening the physical network that supports broadband and other digital communication services.
The expansion of optical fibre infrastructure is important for extending connectivity beyond major urban centres. Fibre networks provide the backbone for high-capacity data transmission and can support broadband access, public services and digital infrastructure in rural and remote areas.
The dashboard also recorded growth in broadband subscriptions during 2025-26. Wired broadband subscribers increased by 12.4 percent, while wireless broadband subscribers grew by 12.9 percent.
The number of connected Gram Panchayats reached 2,23,814 by August 2026. A total of 5,352 Gram Panchayats were added during the first five months of the current financial year.
These indicators capture different aspects of digital connectivity: the expansion of physical infrastructure, growth in broadband subscriptions and the reach of connectivity at the local governance level.
The figures point to continued expansion of India’s telecommunications network, although they do not independently establish the quality, affordability or consistency of services available to individual users.
Air cargo traffic grows 12 percent
India’s civil aviation sector also recorded an increase in freight movement. Airports handled 18.6 lakh tonnes of air cargo during April-August 2026-27, representing year-on-year growth of 12 percent.
Delhi airport handled the highest volume, accounting for 5.3 lakh tonnes during the period.
Air cargo is an important component of logistics infrastructure, supporting the movement of time-sensitive goods, high-value products and other shipments that require faster transportation. Growth in cargo volumes can reflect increased activity across supply chains, trade and distribution networks, although the dashboard figures do not identify the specific factors behind the rise.
Foreign tourist arrivals also increased during the period. India recorded 30.49 lakh foreign tourist arrivals up to August in the current financial year, marking a 2 percent increase compared with the corresponding period a year earlier.
The growth in air cargo and foreign tourist arrivals presents two separate indicators of activity in the aviation and travel ecosystem. While cargo volumes increased at a faster rate, tourist arrivals recorded more modest growth.
The data provides a snapshot of sectoral activity during the first five months of the financial year rather than a full-year assessment.
Major ports handle 390.4 million tonnes of cargo
Port infrastructure recorded growth in cargo handling during April-August 2026-27. Major ports handled 390.4 million tonnes of cargo, registering a year-on-year increase of 7.2 percent.
Non-major ports handled 313.4 million tonnes during the same period, marking growth of 1.8 percent.
The figures show that cargo volumes increased across both categories, although the growth rate at major ports was higher. Ports remain important to India’s trade and logistics network, facilitating the movement of fuel, industrial inputs, raw materials and other commodities.
Petroleum and crude products remained the largest commodity category at major ports, accounting for approximately 29.2 percent of total cargo handled. Cargo movement in this category grew by 3.1 percent year-on-year.
The commodity mix highlights the continued importance of petroleum-related shipments in port activity. At the same time, overall cargo handling depends on demand across multiple sectors and commodity groups.
The latest figures offer an indication of port utilisation and cargo movement during the period, but do not by themselves establish changes in port efficiency, turnaround times or the cost of transporting goods.
Installed power capacity crosses 532 GW
India’s installed power capacity reached 5,32,739.7 megawatts in 2025-26, recording year-on-year growth of 12.1 percent, according to the dashboard.
Renewable energy capacity increased by 29.5 percent to 2,23,273 megawatts, accounting for approximately 42 percent of the country’s total installed power capacity.
The growth in renewable capacity outpaced the increase in overall installed capacity, highlighting the expanding contribution of renewable energy sources to India’s electricity infrastructure.
Installed capacity represents the maximum electricity generation capacity available under specified conditions. It is different from the actual amount of electricity generated, which depends on factors including weather, fuel availability, plant performance and demand.
The figures therefore indicate an expansion in the country’s electricity generation infrastructure, particularly in renewable energy, rather than measuring the actual share of renewables in electricity generation during the year.
The increase in capacity is an important indicator of infrastructure development, while the broader performance of the power sector also depends on transmission networks, distribution systems, reliability and affordability.
Railways add to infrastructure capacity
Indian Railways also recorded growth in its infrastructure and rolling stock during 2024-25.
The number of railway coaches increased by 4.5 percent, while the locomotive fleet grew by 6.4 percent. The length of electrified railway tracks rose by 4.8 percent, and the number of railway wagons increased by 5.4 percent.
These indicators cover different components of railway capacity. Coaches support passenger services, locomotives provide traction, electrified tracks enable electric train operations on covered routes, and wagons are used to transport freight.
Growth across these categories points to an expansion of railway assets and supporting infrastructure. However, the number of coaches, locomotives and wagons does not by itself measure service quality or operational performance. Factors such as network congestion, utilisation, punctuality and freight movement also affect the overall effectiveness of the railway system.
The figures nevertheless provide a snapshot of additions to the physical resources available to the national rail network.
PAIMANA dashboard expands to 184 indicators
The latest quarterly update has expanded the PAIMANA dashboard to 184 indicators, with 21 new indicators added to the platform. Quarterly data for 41 indicators has also been updated across selected infrastructure sectors.
The dashboard tracks six infrastructure sub-sectors: civil aviation; road transport and highways; power; ports, shipping and waterways; telecommunications; and railways.
Its indicators are organised around five dimensions: access, quality, fiscal cost and revenue, utilisation, and affordability. This structure allows infrastructure performance to be examined through more than just the amount of physical capacity created.
For instance, the length of a road network reflects infrastructure availability, while toll transactions provide an indication of usage. Similarly, installed power capacity measures generation potential, whereas broadband subscriptions provide information about connectivity uptake.

articles.title: What is holding up the US-India trade deal? - Kuwait Times
articles.summary: What is holding up the US-India trade deal?  Kuwait Times
articles.full_text:
MUMBAI, India: US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is set to visit India for the second time this year as Washington seeks to shore up ties with a strategic partner despite months of friction over a trade deal. Rubio will meet senior Indian officials, but will skip New Delhi on this trip. Instead he will focus on investment and energy, with visits to the financial hub of Mumbai and the oil hub of Jamnagar. Jamnagar is home to billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s refining complex, the world’s largest.
Experts say the elephant in the room will be the two countries’ failure to seal their long-awaited trade deal. Several factors have made it harder for negotiators to clinch an agreement: US President Donald Trump’s tariff blitz, friction over energy imports and Washington’s warmer ties with Pakistan, India’s arch-rival. According to the US State Department, Rubio’s six-day overseas trip begins on Saturday in Uzbekistan, before he travels on to India.
Here are some of the challenges the trade pact has faced, and the road ahead.
Why has the deal been delayed? In February, India and the United States agreed on a framework for an interim deal. Under it, Washington would lower reciprocal tariffs from 25 percent to 18 percent, and India would cut duties on a range of industrial and agricultural goods. After months of negotiations, the agreement has still not been finalized and signed.
One reason is legal uncertainty over Trump’s tariff plans, after court challenges undermined the reciprocal tariffs the framework was built on. “The February framework had offered to reduce India’s reciprocal tariff… in return for substantial Indian concessions. Once that tariff regime was struck down, the value of the US offer became unclear,” trade expert Ajay Srivastava said in a note.
India is also wary of new US trade measures that could affect it. These include an investigation into alleged unfair trade practices in several countries, and a new law that allows tariffs of up to 100 percent on countries that buy Russian oil. On Friday, Trump signed an executive order waiving those threatened sanctions.
Where do negotiations stand? Progress appears to have hit several hurdles. For most of this year, both governments spoke optimistically about finalizing the interim deal. In June, US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said negotiators were working on the “last one percent” of the pact.
More recently, the tone has become markedly cautious. Last week, Indian Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said talks had hit a “plateau”, with little room for further concessions. Her remarks came days after US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said an announcement was not “imminent”.
What are the main sticking points? Agriculture remains a sensitive area for India, which is reluctant to expose its farmers to more foreign competition. Washington, for its part, wants India to buy more US energy.
New Delhi has also insisted that its final tariff rate must be competitive with the rates given to regional manufacturing rivals such as Vietnam. This week, Indian Trade Minister Piyush Goyal said the first tranche of the deal was in its final stages. But he added that it would not take effect until India secured an edge over its competitors. “It’s going through the final contours, the legal drafting, and we hope to be able to finalize that soon and operationalize that once we get competitive advantage over our peer countries,” he said.
How has trade held up? India’s goods exports to the US jumped 21 percent in August to $8.3 billion, compared with the same month a year earlier, when India faced 50 percent tariffs. The surge in exports has been a bright spot for the Indian economy, which has been hit by high energy prices caused by war in the Middle East. Economists say that if higher tariffs returned, they would cloud India’s growth outlook, hurt market sentiment and add pressure on an already weak rupee. — AFP

Proposed centre will connect academic research with industry, creating opportunities for internships, work placements and collaborative projects.
NEW DELHI, Oct 16: The University of Manchester has announced plans to establish a centre in Bengaluru to strengthen its engagement with India and expand collaboration with students, researchers, businesses and alumni. The proposed facility aims to build closer links between higher education, scientific research and the country’s rapidly developing technology and innovation sectors.
The announcement was made during the university’s engagement with India as part of a delegation representing universities, businesses, civic leaders and cultural organisations from northern England. The initiative is intended to deepen academic and commercial partnerships while creating opportunities for practical learning and research collaboration.
Bengaluru has been selected as the preferred location because of its established position as a major hub for technology, higher education, research and innovation. The city also hosts a strong network of international companies, start-ups and research institutions, making it a suitable location for connecting university expertise with industry requirements.
According to the university, the proposed centre will build on existing relationships with Indian organisations and provide a platform for wider engagement with employers, students and academic communities. Its activities are expected to support industry-linked projects, internships and work placements, helping students gain experience beyond traditional classroom learning.
Connecting academic learning with industry
One of the central objectives of the proposed centre is to bring academic knowledge closer to real-world professional challenges. The university plans to draw on its Partner-Enabled Learning (PEL) model, which incorporates projects involving employers, public bodies and community organisations into degree programmes.
The approach is designed to help students develop practical abilities alongside subject knowledge. These include problem-solving, teamwork, adaptability and the capacity to apply theoretical concepts to professional situations.
Through closer cooperation with industry, students may gain exposure to the expectations of employers and the skills needed in changing workplaces. Such engagement can also help academic institutions understand emerging industry requirements and incorporate relevant experiences into teaching and research.
The proposed facility is expected to provide a focal point for these interactions, although the university has not announced a complete operational timetable or detailed programme list for the Bengaluru centre.
The initiative also reflects the growing importance of collaboration between universities and employers in preparing graduates for a competitive employment market. Practical projects and professional placements can help students understand workplace responsibilities while allowing organisations to engage with emerging talent.
Bengaluru’s growing role in higher education
The choice of Bengaluru highlights the city’s significance in India’s education and technology landscape. Its concentration of technology companies, research organisations and higher education institutions offers opportunities for partnerships across multiple disciplines.
For international universities, establishing a local presence can provide a more direct route to engagement with Indian students, researchers and employers. It can also help institutions develop long-term relationships with businesses and public organisations operating in the country.
The University of Manchester already has partnerships with Indian companies, including Reliance, Tata and Infosys. The proposed centre is expected to build on these existing connections and broaden cooperation across research, professional learning and innovation.
The university’s decision comes amid wider efforts by international higher education institutions to strengthen their engagement with India. Academic collaboration, research partnerships and links with employers have become important areas of cooperation as universities seek to expand their global reach.
However, the proposed Bengaluru facility should not automatically be interpreted as a new degree-awarding campus. The announcement focuses on strengthening engagement and collaboration; specific details about courses, admissions, staffing and the centre’s operational structure have yet to be established publicly.
Opportunities for students and researchers
The planned centre could provide a platform for students and researchers to engage with organisations working on practical problems in technology, business and other research-intensive fields.
Internships and work placements are particularly valuable because they allow students to apply classroom knowledge in professional settings. Exposure to project deadlines, teamwork, client requirements and workplace communication can help graduates prepare for employment.
Collaborative research can also benefit universities and businesses. Academic researchers may gain access to industry challenges and potential partners, while companies can draw on university expertise to explore new ideas, improve processes and develop innovative solutions.
The proposed facility may strengthen these links by creating a local point of contact for stakeholders who want to work with the university. The precise opportunities available to individual students, however, will depend on programmes and partnerships announced as the initiative develops.
Students interested in future collaborations should follow official university announcements for information about activities, eligibility requirements and application procedures. The announcement does not itself confirm the availability of specific internships or scholarships.
Building on international partnerships
The University of Manchester has international centres in Dubai, Hong Kong, Shanghai and Singapore. Its proposed Bengaluru presence would extend its engagement network and reinforce its focus on international cooperation.
The announcement aligns with the institution’s broader global strategy, which emphasises international partnerships and engagement with research, business and cultural communities.
The university’s president and vice-chancellor, Professor Duncan Ivison, said the institution had a longstanding relationship with India across education, business and culture. He described the proposed centre as an important step towards deepening those connections.
The announcement was made at an event at Science Gallery Bengaluru, attended by Greater Manchester Mayor Bev Craig and university representatives. Discussions at the event included innovation and culture, reflecting the range of areas in which the institution seeks to strengthen its engagement with India.
The initiative also coincided with the first Great North Mayoral Mission to India, held from October 12 to 16. The delegation brought together representatives from universities, businesses, civic institutions and cultural organisations in northern England to explore closer cooperation with Indian partners.
Wider implications for higher education
The proposed centre comes at a time when universities are increasingly expected to demonstrate how academic programmes prepare students for professional careers and contribute to research and innovation.
Closer university-industry partnerships can help address the gap between theoretical instruction and workplace expectations. They can also support the development of new ideas by bringing researchers into contact with businesses seeking solutions to technical and commercial challenges.
For Indian institutions and companies, international partnerships may provide additional avenues for research cooperation, knowledge exchange and professional development. Such collaborations can also create opportunities for academic staff to work with colleagues across countries and disciplines.
At the same time, the impact of the proposed centre will depend on how effectively its activities are developed and made accessible. Clear information about partnerships, programmes and opportunities will be necessary for students and researchers seeking to participate.
The university has not yet announced detailed admission arrangements, a formal launch date or a complete list of activities for the facility. Further announcements will be needed to establish the centre’s operational scope and the specific opportunities it will offer.
Next steps
The planned Bengaluru centre represents a new phase in the University of Manchester’s engagement with India, with a focus on connecting academic expertise to practical research and industry needs.
By building on existing corporate relationships and adopting a learning model that incorporates real-world projects, the institution aims to strengthen links between education and employment.
For students, researchers and businesses, the key development to watch will be the release of further details explaining how the centre will operate and how participants can access its activities. Its long-term contribution will depend on the partnerships established, the quality of collaborative projects and the opportunities created for meaningful academic and professional engagement.
