Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said the first phase of the India-US trade pact has been finalised and is now in legal drafting. He added it would be operationalised once India secures a competitive advantage over peer countries. He also said the India-European Union free trade agreement could be signed in December.
Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal said the first phase of the India-US trade pact was finalised. Goyal said the text was now in legal drafting before it could be put into effect. Goyal linked implementation to India getting a tariff edge over comparable countries. The comments were made at the SRCC Centenary Conclave on Thursday.
Goyal said the position on the proposed deal had not shifted over time. Goyal said the remarks matched earlier statements made in recent months. "US bilateral trade agreements first tranche has been finalised, and it is going through final contours, the legal drafting, and we hope to be able to finalise that soon and operationalise that once we get the comparable advantage or competitive advantage over our peer countries,\" Goyal said.
India-US trade pact legal drafting and tariff advantage
Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said talks with the US were progressing well. \"Probably we are in a very good zone. We anticipate closing the deal and signing the deal at the earliest possible time,\" Agrawal told reporters. Agrawal said the agreement timing depended on US work to formalise an overall tariff structure.
Agrawal said parallel work was underway in the US to restore tariff structures. Agrawal said outcomes under Section 301 would shape the next steps. \"So, there is parallel work being done in the US also to get back the tariff structure and based on some of the outcomes under Section 301, we will progress towards signing the deal at a mutually agreed time,\" Agrawal said.
Agrawal said legal drafting was continuing, with focus on preferential access. Agrawal said trade pacts matter because they improve market access on both sides. \"The idea is when you do a trade deal, the trade deal has also a very important component that it gives you not only market access in each others market, it gives you preferential market access in each others market,\" Agrawal said.
Agrawal said India wanted preferential terms compared with competitors in the US market. \"So in that context, India has to get preferential market access with their competitors. And that is something which will come as a part of the new tariff framework that the US is working on,\" Agrawal said. India has sought better tariffs than rivals for Indian goods.
India-US trade pact and Section 301 issues
Asked about concerns linked to Section 301 investigations on excess capacity, Agrawal said issues would be addressed. \"I think all other issues will get settled as part of the deal,\" Agrawal said. Earlier this month, India and 14 other countries urged joint global steps against excess industrial output.
On the same issue, Agrawal said India had opposed capacity built through non-market measures. \"Excess capacity due to non-market forces or non-market interventions has been something which India has also been opposing in a big way,\" Agrawal said. Agrawal added such policies harm global trade and disrupt supply and demand balance.
Agrawal was also asked about the US Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026. The measure allows US President Donald Trump to impose tariffs up to 100 per cent. It targets the biggest buyers of Russian oil and gas. \"Hopefully when it pact is signed, hopefully we will have more clarification on that.\"
Agrawal said India would seek steadier tariff and trade conditions through the agreement. Agrawal did not confirm if the Act would be part of the US tariff framework. Agrawal said clarity may come when the pact is signed. The government has linked the deal to stability in duties and trade flows.
India-US trade pact status and diplomatic timeline
Earlier this month, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the deal was not close. \"At the same time...I dont think theres something imminent, but we truly have identified the universe of items that are sticking points. Were working diligently towards them,\" Greer said. Agrawal said the set of issues had narrowed over time.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio will travel to India next week. The framework for the first tranche was announced in February. Later shifts in the US tariff landscape led to further negotiations. On October 5, Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman said talks were still on, but both sides had hit a plateau.

US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor said talks were progressing quickly. Gor said major items were already settled. \"I wont like to get into too many details at this stage, and let the ministers announce that. India’s semiconductor ecosystem is gradually taking shape, with 12 approved projects across six states attracting committed investments of more than ₹1.64 lakh crore, former NITI Aayog CEO and G20 Sherpa Amitabh Kant said on Monday.

"6 states and 12 approved projects, backed by ₹1.64 lakh crore+ in committed investments. India’s semiconductor future is taking shape!" he stated.
Gujarat hosts several major semiconductor investments, led by Tata-PSMC’s semiconductor fabrication plant at Dholera. The project involves an investment of ₹91,526 crore and is designed to have a planned production capacity exceeding 50,000 wafers per month.
Another major project is Micron Technology’s assembly and test facility at Sanand, which will handle DRAM and NAND products. The facility involves an investment of ₹22,516 crore.
The state is also home to the CG Power-Renesas-Stars semiconductor outsourced semiconductor assembly and test (OSAT) facility, which has an investment of ₹7,584 crore.
Other approved projects in Gujarat include facilities being developed by Kaynes Semicon, Crystal Matrix and Suchi Semicon. These projects cover areas such as semiconductor packaging, compound semiconductors, mini-LED technologies and discrete semiconductor manufacturing.
The concentration of projects across different segments could help Gujarat develop a broader semiconductor manufacturing ecosystem, linking fabrication with assembly, testing and specialised component production.
Assam is another important location in India’s semiconductor expansion. Tata Semiconductor Assembly and Test is developing an OSAT and packaging facility in the state with an investment of ₹27,120 crore.
The proposed facility is expected to have a capacity of around 48 million units per day. The project will expand the geographical spread of semiconductor manufacturing beyond the Western Industrial Corridor.
Assembly and testing facilities are an important part of the semiconductor supply chain, helping process and package chips manufactured through fabrication facilities.
Odisha has secured two approved projects focused on specialised semiconductor technologies and advanced packaging.
SiCSem is developing a silicon carbide fabrication and packaging facility involving an investment of ₹2,066 crore. Silicon carbide is used in power electronics and applications requiring high efficiency and performance under demanding operating conditions.

Together, the projects add specialised manufacturing capabilities to the state’s industrial ecosystem.
Andhra Pradesh is hosting an Advanced System in Package (ASIP) facility focused on system-in-package technologies. The project involves an investment of about ₹480 crore and has a proposed annual capacity of nearly 96 million units.
Punjab is also part of the emerging semiconductor network. CDIL is developing a power semiconductor project involving an investment of ₹117 crore.
The projects illustrate the range of technologies being pursued across states, from semiconductor fabrication and packaging to power devices and advanced integration.
The 12 approved projects across six states represent a significant investment commitment towards building India’s semiconductor ecosystem. Their development spans fabrication, assembly, testing, packaging and specialised chip technologies.
As these projects progress, their implementation and production capabilities will be important factors in determining how quickly India can expand domestic semiconductor manufacturing and strengthen its position in global supply chains.

articles.title: Unresolved border dispute remains principal obstacle in India-China relations: Report - MorungExpress

articles.full_text:
Chinese President Xi Jinping walks around the Monument to the People's Heroes to pay tribute during a ceremony to present flower baskets to fallen national heroes at Tian'anmen Square in Beijing, capital of China, Sept. 30, 2026. Xi Jinping and other leaders of the Communist Party of China and the state including Li Qiang, Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang, Li Xi and Han Zheng attended the ceremony on Wednesday. The event was held to mark Martyrs' Day. Observed on Sept. 30, one day before National Day, the day commemorates those who gave their lives for national independence and prosperity. (Photo: Xinhua via IANS)
Beijing, October 19 (IANS): The unresolved border dispute remains a central security concern and the principal obstacle in India-China relations which are still short of their pre-2020 status quo despite Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to New Delhi last month for the BRICS summit prompting speculation that both countries are moving toward a reset, a report has highlighted.
India has sought to stabilise ties and manage differences with China since the 2020 Galwan clashes with the efforts gaining momentum due to US President Donald Trump’s increasingly hostile policies toward India and much of Asia, a report in The Diplomat highlighted.
However, Xi's New Delhi visit for the BRICS Summit in September and the bilateral meeting with Prime Minister Narendra Modi should not be mistaken for an alignment of interests, the report cautioned.
"The resumption of high-level dialogue, leadership meetings, and direct connectivity are important developments. Another Galwan-like border confrontation would carry heavy domestic costs and could be difficult to recover from. Preventing a recurrence of such violence is a priority. But this does not require India to reconsider its position on the underlying differences," wrote Sana Hashmi, a fellow at the Taiwan-Asia Exchange Foundation.
"It is also important to note that India never abandoned dialogue with China after Galwan. Keeping communication channel open has remained part of its approach, even as tensions persisted along the border. The latest meetings continue that policy; they do not demonstrate that the relationship or India's approach to it has fundamentally changed," Hashmi mentioned.
The report mentioned that China's recent statement that it does not recognise the Union Territory of Ladakh, underlines the depth of the disagreement.
"There is little basis for expecting a reset while the two sides remain so far apart on territorial issues. Nor is the border the only source of friction. China’s relationship with Pakistan and the persistent trade imbalance remain contentious issues, too. There is little evidence of progress on any of these fundamental differences," it added.
The Diplomat report stated that the Galwan clashes changed India’s view of and threat perception from China and raised serious questions about the viability of the existing arrangements in ensuring peace along the Line of Actual Control (LAC).
"High-level meetings can help manage tensions for the time being, but they cannot substitute for progress on the ground. India is also unlikely to return to its previous position on the One China policy without some reference to, or assurance regarding, a corresponding One India policy from Beijing. Such an assurance appears unlikely in the foreseeable future," Hashmi opined.
"Just a couple of years ago, a meeting between Xi and Modi on Indian soil seemed difficult to imagine. That is one of the reasons why their meeting drew so much attention. But it has not changed the scope or nature of the issues dividing the two countries. For now, both sides are trying to prevent another crisis while their core disagreements remain unresolved. Until those differences are addressed, dialogue may keep the relationship from deteriorating further, but it will not put China-India ties on the path to a reset," the expert added.
During their meeting on the sidelines of the BRICS Summit in New Delhi on September 12, PM Modi had reiterated to Xi Jinping that India and China should show sensitivity to each other's core concerns and be guided by mutual respect, mutual interest and mutual sensitivity.
Both leaders had emphasised that "differences should not become disputes" and reaffirmed that the two countries should take a strategic and long term perspective of their ties.
"The two leaders welcomed the steady progress in India-China bilateral relations since their last meeting in Tianjin in August 2025. They reaffirmed that both countries should take a strategic and long term perspective of their ties. Differences should not become disputes. Prime Minister highlighted that both sides must be guided by three mutuals- mutual respect, mutual sensitivity and mutual interest," read a statement issued by the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA) after the meeting.

articles.title: The West’s transactional pivot to India - GIS Reports
articles.summary: The West’s transactional pivot to India  GIS Reports
articles.full_text:
The West is courting India for trade, minerals, technology and defense – and, above all, to break China’s grip on supply chains.
GIS Radio
Listen to our AI-powered podcast for comprehensive insights.
- The EU’s new FTA with India is a geoeconomic tool binding them together
- U.S. broadens its security approach with India into major commercial ties
- De-risking with India is slow, with full political alignment unlikely
While the United States and the European Union have traditionally approached India through largely distinct prisms – Washington through a security-centric lens and Brussels with a regulatory-trade focus – the core objective of both strategies is practically identical. The Western powers are engaged in a sophisticated, albeit sometimes clumsy, campaign to court India to secure critical minerals, high-tech manufacturing partnerships and supply chain alternatives. This is less a geopolitical love affair and more a transactional necessity driven by the realization that the West cannot reduce its dependence on China by itself; it needs India and other middle powers.
India is particularly attractive to the West because of the size and growth of its economy, its large industrial and technological base, substantial labor force and capability in becoming both a major supplier and end-market. Although the European and American approaches differ in emphasis, both are attempting to persuade India that deeper economic integration with the West can serve India’s interests as well as their own.
The EU’s regulatory and trade approach
Brussels has made the clearest trade-led effort to cultivate India. In January 2026, the EU and India concluded negotiations on a landmark free trade agreement (FTA) after years of difficult talks. The two sides plan to sign it in December 2026 and to bring it into force in early 2027. The European Commission called it the largest trade agreement either side has ever concluded. India will eliminate or reduce tariffs on 96.6 percent of EU goods exports by value.
Yet the agreement’s significance goes beyond tariff cuts. Bilateral trade totaled 192 billion euros in 2025, and the EU is India’s third-largest trading partner. The bloc’s foreign direct investment stock in India reached 132 billion euros in 2024, making the EU the country’s leading foreign investor. The FTA therefore seeks to move an already substantial relationship toward deeper economic integration.
The EU’s economic-security strategy increasingly treats trade policy as a tool for building strategic resilience. The goal is not simply to sell more European goods and services in India, but also to build more diversified production networks. The European and Indian economies are complementary: Europe has sophisticated industrial technology, capital and high-value manufacturing capabilities, while India offers a large domestic market, a growing manufacturing base, engineering expertise and a vast pool of skilled workers.
Even so, one point of disagreement reveals underlying tensions. New Delhi views Europe’s carbon border adjustment mechanism (CBAM) with deep suspicion. The mechanism imposes a carbon charge on imports of carbon-intensive goods such as steel and aluminum. Indian negotiators see CBAM as protectionism dressed in green clothing, a direct threat to India’s nascent industrial base.
The FTA does not exempt India from CBAM, and the EU has said India will receive no more favorable CBAM treatment than any other country. However, the EU has offered technical assistance to help Indian industries decarbonize, effectively offering financial aid to help their steelmakers meet European standards. The EU is using its regulatory power, backed by the promise of market access, to reshape India’s industrial policy.
Brussels’ critical minerals ambitions
The EU’s most pressing resource need is securing raw materials for the energy transition without deepening its dependence on China, which dominates processing of most critical minerals. Individual member states have signed their own critical minerals agreements with New Delhi: Memorandums of Understanding (MoUs) with Italy and the Netherlands, and a Joint Declaration of Intent with Germany. They cover exploration, processing, recycling and supply-chain resilience.
India’s critical-mineral potential is real but unproven. In 2023, the Geological Survey of India reported 5.9 million metric tons of inferred lithium-bearing ore in Jammu and Kashmir, its first major lithium find. India also holds licenses to explore Indian Ocean seabed nodules containing nickel, copper and cobalt. Developing these will take years of investment in exploration, extraction and processing, where Europe could help with technology and finance. In return, the EU might seek long-term supply agreements.
The EU is also backing a proposed “Critical Minerals Club” to set common standards for responsible mining and processing. Helping India build a sustainable mining sector would give Europe an alternative supply chain less exposed to China: capital and technology today in exchange for secure raw-material flows tomorrow.
Europe’s semiconductor gambit
Beyond minerals, Europe is looking to India for high-tech resilience. The European Chips Act aims to double the EU’s share of the global semiconductor market by 2030. However, Europe lacks the fabrication capacity and skilled workforce to reach that target on its own. The EU has therefore turned to India, whose semiconductor mission has moved into a second phase with an approved budget of about $13 billion.
In early 2023, the EU launched a Trade and Technology Council (TTC) with India, its second such forum after the one it set up with the U.S. In November 2023, under the TTC, the two sides signed an MoU on semiconductor ecosystems, supply chains and innovation. At the 2025 TTC meeting, the EU and India discussed cooperation on semiconductors, solar technology, pharmaceuticals, critical technologies and other strategic sectors. Such cooperation serves a dual purpose for Europe: It reduces the continent’s reliance on Chinese-made chips for automobiles and, by training Indian engineers to European standards, binds India more closely to Europe’s technological ecosystem.
Washington’s turn to trade
Washington’s relationship with New Delhi has traditionally been shaped by strategic and security considerations, particularly through defense cooperation in the form of the Quad, broader Indo-Pacific security and technology partnerships. Nevertheless, the economic dimension has grown in importance. In February 2025, the U.S. and India announced Mission 500, which aims to more than double bilateral trade to $500 billion by 2030. They also opened negotiations on a bilateral trade agreement intended to improve market access, reduce tariff and nontariff barriers and integrate the two economies more closely.
Since then, the path has been turbulent. After imposing 50 percent tariffs on Indian goods in August 2025, partly over India’s purchases of Russian oil, Washington agreed in February 2026 to cut them to 18 percent under an interim trade framework. Later that month, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the tariffs. Most Indian exports now face a 10 percent duty, and the interim deal remains unsigned.
The negotiations reflect both opportunity and tension. America has long complained that India’s tariff regime and regulatory barriers make it harder for U.S. companies to access the Indian market than for Indian firms to enter the American market. Washington’s negotiators have therefore approached India not only as a geopolitical partner but also as a commercial counterpart whose market they want to open further to American exporters.
America’s critical minerals push
Critical minerals provide a particularly clear bridge between the security and economic dimensions of the U.S.-India relationship. In May 2026, the two countries established a Strategic Critical Minerals Cooperation Framework to deepen cooperation in mining, processing, recycling and financing.
New Delhi is seeking to reduce vulnerabilities in strategic raw materials while developing domestic exploration, processing and recycling capacity. The U.S. Department of Commerce notes that India has allocated significant public resources to developing its critical-minerals sector and has identified substantial opportunities to use American mining equipment, services, technology and investment.
Thus, the U.S. objective is not simply to extract Indian minerals. A more sustainable model would involve U.S. capital and technology helping India build domestic value chains, with Indian firms subsequently integrating into wider American production networks.

- The coevolution of sanctions and a multipolar world order
Economic weight, diplomatic independence
A broader political calculation underpins this Western economic courtship. India is increasingly important in global economic governance and is one of the few countries with enough economic weight to shape international supply chains while maintaining considerable diplomatic independence. As a result, the EU and the U.S. have expanded cooperation with India across trade, technology, connectivity, defense and global governance. In 2025, European and Indian officials discussed mutual economic security, resilient supply chains, trade and investment, infrastructure connectivity, the EU’s Global Gateway and the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor.
“Courting India” is not simply a contest for Indian allegiance. articles.title: Is Europe having its Arab Spring moment? Are protests in 9 countries linked? - India Today
articles.summary: Is Europe having its Arab Spring moment? Are protests in 9 countries linked?  India TodayFrom France to Albania, social unrest is setting Europe’s streets ablaze  The HinduWhy are people protesting across Europe?  The GuardianAre Europe's cost-of-living protests spiraling out of control?  CGTNHow has the cost of living changed in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal?  Al Jazeera
articles.full_text:
From France and Italy to Albania, a wave of violent protests has gripped at least nine European countries. Demonstrations, with similar grievances, have turned violent in several cities. Amid this, comparisons are being drawn with the Arab Spring, which saw the fall of several authoritarian regimes in the Middle East and Africa. What do experts say about the movements in Europe? Are they connected?
At a time when wars, economic uncertainty and political divisions are unsettling the world, a storm has hit Europe's streets. A wave of protests, some descending into riots and violence, has prompted comparisons with the Arab Spring, the wave of uprisings that began in Tunisia in late 2010 and swept across the Middle East and North Africa, toppling several long-entrenched rulers.
Now, in 2026, from Paris and Milan to Madrid and Tirana, protesters are challenging governments over rising living costs, unaffordable housing, deteriorating education and political corruption. Demonstrations have turned violent in France, Italy, Belgium and Albania, while other countries are witnessing strikes, school occupations and growing student mobilisation.
At least nine European countries have seen protests. They include France, Italy, Belgium and Austria, where concerns about education cuts triggered unrest.
In Spain, Portugal and Greece, protesters raised concerns over soaring housing costs. Students in Germany are opposing military-service plans. Demonstrators in Albania are protesting against corruption and unemployment.
With the demonstrations turning violent in some countries, the unrest in Europe has drawn comparisons with the Arab Spring, which began in December 2010.
However, experts have cautioned against treating the protests across at least nine European countries as a single, coordinated uprising. They say grievances and demands differ from one nation to another. Unlike the Arab Spring, which saw mass uprisings against authoritarian rulers and brought down several governments, Europe's protests are unfolding largely within established democracies, with demonstrators primarily demanding reforms rather than the overthrow of entire political systems.
Over the October 16-18 weekend, hundreds of thousands took to the streets across France, where the protests first erupted. Clashes with police, arson and looting in several cities were reported. Agitations took place in Italy, Belgium, Portugal and Albania. Protests were also seen in Austria over education funding, and in Greece over housing costs and university policies.
"France is the epicentre of this movement ... and there are signs now that this is spreading beyond France," Alberto Alemanno, professor of European Union law and policy at HEC Paris, told Al Jazeera. He cautioned that the demonstrations were separate movements, but some shared grievances, including underfunded education, rising living costs and uncertain employment prospects.
But for American-Kuwaiti journalist Ahmed Eldin, Europe's unrest has deeper similarities to the Arab Spring. He said that young people were challenging political elites over economic hardship, inequality and a growing sense of betrayal.
That's what even Indian-American Congressman Ro Khanna suggested, countering US Vice President JD Vance's argument.
While Vance blamed "imported the Third World into France" for the rioting and violence, Khanna linked the protests in France, Spain and Albania to the economic insecurities that the youths faced.
"From the high schools of France to the streets of Madrid to the universities of Tirana, young people are telling their governments the same thing: in an age of massive wealth inequality, they want a future they can believe in," Ro Khanna wrote on X.
FRANCE BECOMES EPICENTRE OF EUROPEAN UNREST
The protests in France began gathering momentum on September 21, when students at Lycee Saint-Exupery in Creteil protested teacher shortages, deteriorating buildings and overcrowded classrooms. The demonstrations subsequently spread, drawing support from trade unions and people struggling with inflation.
On October 17, around 5.5 lakh people participated in 110 demonstrations across France, according to Interior Minister Laurent Nunez. The organisers estimated eight lakh people.
Although most marches were peaceful in several places, violence erupted in Paris, Marseille, Limoges and other French cities. Public buildings were attacked, shops were looted and barricades were set ablaze.
The Associated Press reported approximately 400 arrests on October 17.
French President Emmanuel Macron slammed what he called "unbridled" violence and asked, "How could the French people do this to France?"
The unrest also became a political battleground over immigration. On October 6, US President Donald Trump blamed France's student protests on migration, saying, "This isn't about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great country!"
French far-right leader Marine Le Pen blamed decades of uncontrolled immigration.
ITALY AND BELGIUM ALSO SEE CLASHES
Italian students staged demonstrations on October 16, protesting education funding, military expenditure and government policies. In Turin and Rome, some students occupied schools, borrowing tactics from their French counterparts.
At the October 16 "No Meloni Day" protests in Italy, students marched against a proposed cap on foreign pupils in classrooms, raising slogans such as "A scuola nessuno e straniero" ("At school, no one is a foreigner"), alongside demands for increased education funding, Italian news agency ANSA reported.
According to a new national decree, the government of Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has capped the number of non-Italian students to 30% in some classes. Meloni had also said she would bring a measure to ban the wearing of burqas and niqabs in schools.
On October 17, demonstrations in Milan escalated when masked protesters threw stones and paving blocks at police and set barricades ablaze.
Belgium also witnessed protests against education cuts, higher fees and economic pressures. Police deployed water cannon during disturbances in Liege. Belgian Interior Minister Bernard Quintin described some incidents as "pure and simple violence", reported Euronews.
SPAIN AND PORTUGAL FIGHT HOUSING CRISIS
In Spain, housing affordability has become a powerful political grievance. Protests intensified in September following the eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, whose rent had reportedly increased sharply. Her subsequent death intensified anger over evictions and property speculation.
In Madrid, students also demonstrated over education, while housing-access activists demanded restrictions on investment funds purchasing residential properties.
Next door, Portugal witnessed major demonstrations in Lisbon on October 17 over rents, wages, pensions and deteriorating public services.
In the early hours of October 15, police allegedly beat protesters while clearing a peaceful housing protest camp in Porto, leaving 37 people injured, including a person with a disability, according to Amnesty International, which demanded an investigation into the reported excessive force.
Europe's housing crisis has particularly impacted the young severely. Many of them have struggled to afford independent accommodation. According to Eurostat data released in September, more than one in four Europeans aged 15 to 29, or 26.9%, lived in overcrowded households in 2025.
ALBANIA'S ANGER TURNS POLITICAL. PROTESTERS WANT PM RAMA TO RESIGN
Albania presented a different picture. Here, protests were driven less by economic hardship and more by longstanding anger over alleged government corruption, unemployment and demands for PM Edi Rama's resignation.
On October 17, thousands of young demonstrators gathered outside Tirana's Education Ministry, demanding Prime Minister Edi Rama's resignation. It was the fifth consecutive day of a growing student-led movement.
Reuters reported that masked protesters threw stones at riot police, who responded with tear gas, stun grenades and water cannon.
The unrest in Albania followed months of anger over alleged corruption, unemployment and a controversial coastal development associated with Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law.
Unlike demonstrations elsewhere in Europe, Albania's protests directly challenged the Rama government's continuation in office. Despite the demands, Edi Rama has refused to step down, accusing his opponents of exploiting the unrest to destabilise his government.
GERMANY, AUSTRIA AND GREECE ALSO SEE MOBILISATION
Germany, Austria and Greece bring the number of European countries witnessing protests or student mobilisation to nine. However, the scale and intensity of demonstrations in these three countries have been considerably lower than the countries we discussed.
In Berlin, students blockaded entrances to Andreas-Gymnasium on October 16, opposing preparations for compulsory military service and demanding greater investment in education. The protesters also expressed solidarity with students demonstrating in France.
In Austria, students mobilised against university budget cuts and concerns over deteriorating educational facilities. Greece, meanwhile, witnessed student anger over soaring accommodation costs, private universities, housing shortages and increased military spending.
Speaking to Al Jazeera, European Union law professor Alberto Alemanno said, "In Greece, students are also calling for walkouts and they are mobilising in Germany. In Austria, we also see the early stage of a movement with mobilisation expected in the coming week."
However, Alemanno cautioned against portraying the unrest as a coordinated uprising, saying, "This is not a single movement. It's more about separate processes happening at the same time with some shared grievances."
